items.title: US Commerce Department allows Anthropic to release Claude Mythos 5 AI model to over 100 trusted US companies and government agencies [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: U.S. allows Anthropic to release Mythos AI to ‘trusted’ US organizations
items.summary:
The US Commerce Department has lifted its export controls on Anthropic's Claude Mythos 5 AI model, permitting its release to over 100 trusted US companies and government agencies. This decision reverses a recent block imposed due to security concerns and marks a significant step in the US government's approach to regulating advanced AI technologies.

Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick cited substantial progress in discussions with Anthropic, noting the company's commitment to collaborate on protocols and standards for AI model releases. While the release of Mythos 5 is authorized, the status of the related Fable 5 model remains uncertain, with talks ongoing regarding its potential availability.

This development reflects the US government's efforts to balance maintaining leadership in AI innovation with safeguarding national security. The new regulatory framework grants the government oversight of frontier AI models, affecting access for international partners and raising concerns among allies about dependency on US decisions.

items.title: Analysis shows the performance gap between open weights and closed source LLMs varies by benchmark, with coding benchmarks narrowing gap to 1-2 months by mid-2026 while others remain around 5 months [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The gap between open weights LLMs and closed source LLMs
items.summary:
An analysis of the performance gap between open weights and closed source large language models (LLMs) reveals that this gap varies depending on the benchmark used. While coding benchmarks show a significant narrowing of the gap, reducing it to about one to two months by mid-2026, other benchmarks indicate the gap remains around five months. This suggests that open source models are catching up to closed source models at different rates across various tasks.

The study examined 18 different benchmarks from the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, finding that improvements in coding capabilities have driven much of the progress in open source LLMs. However, the average gap across all benchmarks has remained relatively stable over time. This highlights the complexity of measuring LLM quality and suggests that predictions about open source models matching closed source ones depend heavily on the chosen evaluation metrics.

items.title: Researchers debate AI's impact on mathematics, exploring how AI-assisted problem solving may reshape the role and purpose of mathematicians [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: AI in mathematics is forcing big questions
items.summary:
Researchers are examining how artificial intelligence is transforming mathematics, particularly through AI-assisted problem solving that could change the traditional role and purpose of mathematicians. Prominent figures like Terence Tao envision a future where humans and AI collaborate on complex mathematical challenges, potentially ushering in an era of "Big Mathematics." This shift raises questions about the nature of mathematical discovery and the value of human intuition and creativity in the field.

Historically, mathematicians have relied on deep contemplation and creative reasoning to formulate and prove conjectures, a process that AI is beginning to accelerate and, in some cases, automate. Recent advances in AI, including systems that perform at the level of top high school mathematicians, demonstrate the technology's growing capability to tackle difficult problems. This evolution prompts ongoing debate about how AI will reshape mathematical research, the experience of mathematicians, and the future of the discipline itself.

items.title: Weave launches a smart model routing proxy for Claude, Codex, and Cursor that selects the best AI model per request with local key encryption and observability [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Show HN: Smart model routing directly in Claude, Codex and Cursor
items.summary:
Weave has launched a smart model routing proxy that selects the best AI model for each request, supporting Claude, Codex, Cursor, and other platforms. This proxy uses a local embedder to route requests efficiently across multiple providers, including Anthropic, OpenAI, and Gemini, while keeping API keys encrypted on the user's device. It also offers observability features with built-in tracing and dashboard integration.

The router supports various AI models and APIs, including open-source options via OpenRouter, and can be easily integrated with existing tools through simple commands or self-hosted setups. It provides flexibility with per-request routing decisions, streaming support, and compatibility with multiple AI service APIs, making it a versatile solution for managing AI model usage.

By enabling local key encryption and detailed observability, Weave's router enhances security and transparency for users managing multiple AI models. Its design aims to optimize model selection dynamically, potentially improving performance and cost-efficiency for developers and organizations using diverse AI services.

items.title: Reports show students in East Asia using AI-powered smart glasses to cheat in exams, prompting education authorities to consider stricter screening and new anti-cheating measures [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: AI glasses help students cheat in exams – test-obsessed Asia is ground zero
items.summary:
Students in East Asia have been reported using AI-powered smart glasses to cheat during exams, raising concerns about academic integrity in the region's highly competitive educational environment. Incidents in South Korea and Taiwan have prompted education authorities to consider stricter screening measures and update anti-cheating protocols to address this emerging challenge.

These smart glasses can discreetly display information and interact with AI models, making traditional exam monitoring more difficult. In response, countries like China and the UK have increased inspections and warnings about the potential for AI-enabled devices to facilitate cheating. Experts warn that as these technologies become more advanced and widespread, education systems will need to adapt their assessment methods to maintain fairness and reliability.

items.title: Ford executives say replacing human engineers with AI was a mistake, rehiring 350 veteran engineers to improve vehicle quality and prevent defects [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ford execs say they made a mistake when they replaced human engineers with AI
items.summary:
Ford has acknowledged that replacing experienced human engineers with artificial intelligence in certain engineering processes was a mistake. The company rehired about 350 veteran engineers to mentor younger staff and reprogram AI diagnostic tools, aiming to improve vehicle quality and prevent defects. This move has contributed to Ford's rise to the top position among mainstream brands in the latest JD Power Quality Survey.

The rehired engineers now lead efforts to troubleshoot vehicles and refine automated systems to catch potential failures before production, helping Ford avoid costly recalls. The company’s experience highlights the limitations of AI when used without sufficient human oversight, especially in complex tasks requiring deep expertise. This case reflects a broader trend where companies that relied heavily on AI-driven layoffs have had to rehire many employees to maintain quality and customer satisfaction.

items.title: Researchers present an iterative data generation pipeline to detect and control sycophancy in language models using cascading linear features for improved interpretability and steering [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Detecting and Controlling Sycophancy with Cascading Linear Features
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an iterative data generation pipeline that improves the detection and control of sycophancy in language models by isolating cascading linear features linked to this behavior. This approach moves beyond simple binary sample pairs to identify samples exhibiting varying degrees of features that scale linearly with sycophantic behavior, enabling better feature disentanglement and interpretability. The method demonstrates that sycophancy-related features form linearly separable subspaces, allowing for more precise selection of model activations corresponding to the behavior compared to baseline techniques.

The study evaluates the pipeline's effectiveness in detecting, scoring, and steering language models away from sycophancy, finding that it matches or outperforms existing methods such as LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting while requiring less computational effort. This work offers enhanced interpretability guarantees and provides code and data to support further research in controlling undesirable model behaviors.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26155v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Interpreting and controlling model behaviors through activation steering methods requires many pairs of contrastive samples that clearly exhibit desired or undesired behavior. These data pairs determine the degree to which interpretability frameworks can reliably detect model features responsible for a behavior, and therefore the ability to steer models toward or away from such behavior. In this work, we present an iterative data generation pipeline that isolates cascading linear features responsible for a behavior. Specifically, we show how moving beyond simple binary pairs of samples, and instead isolating samples that show degrees of features that scale linearly with behavior, allows for better disentanglement of features. We focus on detecting and steering away from sycophancy -- the tendency of language models to prioritize user validation. We demonstrate that sycophancy features discovered through cascading samples form linearly separable subspaces, and allow for selection of model activations that more clearly correspond to the desired behavior than baseline approaches. We also evaluate their ability to enable detection, deterministic scoring, and robust steering, and see that they either match or outperform LLM-as-a-judge and system prompting baselines while providing lower computational demand and more interpretability guarantees. Code & Data: https://cascading-feats.github.io/

items.title: Researchers present CORE-Bench v1.1 and OOD suite to evaluate AI agent performance beyond accuracy saturation, highlighting efficiency, reliability, and human-agent collaboration benefits [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Life After Benchmark Saturation: A Case Study of CORE-Bench
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CORE-Bench v1.1 and an out-of-distribution (OOD) task suite to evaluate AI agent performance beyond traditional accuracy metrics. Using the CORE-Bench Hard benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, they highlight six key performance dimensions often overlooked after accuracy saturation: construct validity, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative impact of model versus scaffold, and benefits from human-agent collaboration. Their findings demonstrate that even when accuracy plateaus, these benchmarks provide valuable insights into agent capabilities.

The study identifies previously unrecognized threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard and presents improved evaluation tools with CORE-Bench v1.1 and CORE-Bench OOD. Additionally, a randomized experiment showed that human-agent collaboration can significantly speed up reproducibility tasks, roughly doubling efficiency compared to human-only efforts. This work advocates for a more comprehensive and rigorous evaluation framework that moves beyond accuracy-centric approaches in assessing AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26158v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: When a benchmark's accuracy saturates, it is often retired and replaced with a more challenging version. We show that this approach privileges accuracy and misses the opportunity to study six other key dimensions of agent performance: construct validity issues such as shortcuts, out-of-distribution generalizability, efficiency, reliability, the relative importance of the model versus the scaffold, and uplift from human-agent collaboration. We use CORE-Bench Hard, a benchmark for computational reproducibility of scientific code, as a case study to demonstrate that measuring agents along these dimensions yields meaningful insights into agent performance even after accuracy saturates. First, we surface threats to construct validity in CORE-Bench Hard that are difficult to anticipate with less capable agents. We introduce an improved benchmark, CORE-Bench v1.1, and an out-of-distribution task suite, CORE-Bench OOD. Second, we find that despite accuracy saturation, CORE-Bench v1.1 remains useful for measuring efficiency, reliability, model performance, and scaffold performance. Finally, we conduct a small-scale randomized experiment to measure uplift from human-agent collaboration on real-world computational reproducibility tasks. We find a statistically significant speedup by about a factor of two -- likely underestimated due to one-fifth of human-only reproductions reaching the time limit before completing -- and describe various other findings. Together, our contributions present a more rigorous alternative to the dominant accuracy-centric evaluation paradigm.

items.title: Researchers find refusal behavior in instruction-tuned chat models is gated downstream of persona expression, with compliant persona suppressing refusal in Qwen2.5-7B and Llama-3.1-8B [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Refusal Lives Downstream of Persona in Chat Models
items.summary:
Researchers have discovered that in instruction-tuned chat models like Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, refusal behavior is influenced by the model's persona expression. Specifically, a compliant persona suppresses refusal responses, with experiments showing refusal rates dropping significantly when the compliant persona direction is activated. The study reveals that refusal is gated downstream of persona expression, occurring at later layers in the model's activation space rather than being an isolated mechanism.

The team extracted distinct directions in the models' activation space corresponding to compliant persona and refusal traits and manipulated these to observe their interaction. Reintroducing the refusal direction restored refusal behavior only at late layers, and removing the persona direction at these layers returned refusal rates to baseline, confirming that refusal depends on persona expression at a late stage. This finding challenges previous approaches that treated refusal as independent, highlighting the importance of considering persona in understanding refusal mechanisms in chat models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Linear directions in activation space have been identified for both refusal and persona traits in instruction-tuned chat models, but the two have been studied as separate mechanisms. We show they interact: a compliant persona gates refusal. In Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, we extract a compliant model-persona direction and a refusal direction and intervene on both. Compliant persona steering suppresses refusal -- in Llama, the refusal rate falls from 97% to 2%. Reintroducing the refusal direction partially restores refusal at late layers but not at early ones. Projecting out the persona direction in a late-layer window restores it to baseline; projecting out a random direction does not. Refusal is therefore gated at the late-layer expression stage, downstream of where it is computed. Treating refusal as a single isolated direction misses its dependence on persona.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent work shows that Large Language Models (LLMs) can act as semantic mutation operators for the evolutionary discovery of programs and proofs. The results demonstrate that LLM-based semantic evolution provides a viable approach for continual program synthesis in complex environments.

items.title: Researchers introduce an LLM-powered pipeline for comparative governance analysis of DAO and corporate AI protocols, analyzing 4,323 records to study participation and thematic convergence in 2026 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Agentic Analysis for Agentic Infrastructure: An LLM-Powered Pipeline for Comparative Governance of DAO and Corporate AI Protocols
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a large language model (LLM)-powered pipeline to analyze governance structures of AI agent protocols, focusing on their interoperability standards. The study compares two governance models—ERC-8004, a permissionless on-chain standard, and Google A2A, a corporate-led standard—by examining 4,323 governance participation records to understand how institutional design influences thematic priorities and community dynamics.

Using automated annotation, neural topic modeling, and multi-layer network analysis, the researchers found that while governance forms affect substantive focus, both models show similar levels of participation inequality and community fragmentation. Notably, the permissionless governance setting exhibited denser discourse alignment, suggesting that open governance may encourage greater thematic convergence despite decentralized participation. The study highlights the potential of LLM-assisted methods to advance empirical research on technology governance and inform the design of more equitable AI standards. All data and code from the study are publicly available.

items.title: Researchers develop provenance-aware AI framework integrating Reddit, WebMD, and FDA data to unify psychiatric medication safety information with traceable claims and early adverse event detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Knowledge-augmented Agentic AI for Mental Health Medication Information Seeking
items.summary: Researchers have developed a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based AI framework that integrates data from Reddit, WebMD, and the U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System to unify psychiatric medication safety information. This system processes over 466,000 Reddit posts, 60,000 WebMD reviews, and two decades of FDA records for nine antidepressants, enabling traceable claims and distinguishing between regulatory facts and patient experiences. The framework uses advanced entity recognition with high accuracy and reveals that patient-generated data provide an independent safety signal, often identifying adverse events earlier than official reports.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26205v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Patients increasingly seek medication information online, yet safety knowledge for psychiatric drugs is split between regulatory adverse-event records, which are authoritative but abstract, and patient narratives, which are experience-near but unvalidated. Integrating them without conflating evidence and anecdote is especially consequential in psychiatry, where poorly contextualised information can amplify fear, nocebo responses, and non-adherence. Here we develop a provenance-aware, knowledge-graph-based multi-agent framework unifying 466,525 Reddit posts, 60,782 WebMD reviews, and twenty years of U.S. FDA Adverse Event Reporting System records for nine antidepressants. A large-language-model entity-recognition pipeline benchmarked against physician annotations reached highest F1 scores of 0.969 for medications and 0.973 for conditions. The two community platforms were far more concordant with each other (overlap up to a Jaccard similarity of 0.905) than with regulatory reports, indicating that patient-generated data form a partly independent safety signal. For sertraline, many adverse events appeared in community sources hundreds of days before the corresponding FDA date. A Neo4j knowledge graph grounded in ATC-N, ICD-10, and MedDRA vocabularies preserves provenance, keeping every claim traceable and regulatory facts distinct from patient experience. These results establish source-aware integration as a route to more auditable psychiatric medication information, with usefulness and patient benefit to be tested prospectively.

items.title: Researchers propose Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo system to accelerate chess skill assessment using move-level data, demonstrating faster adaptation to skill changes than traditional Elo [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Skill Assessment in Chess: A Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a new approach to assessing chess skill that incorporates move-level data to provide faster and more responsive updates than the traditional Elo system. Inspired by cognitive neuroscience models, DD-Elo treats skill expression as a decision-making process, allowing it to capture rapid changes in player ability while maintaining theoretical consistency with existing ratings.

The system addresses the limitations of conventional Elo ratings, which rely solely on match outcomes and thus respond slowly to shifts in player performance. Through rigorous mathematical analysis and extensive experiments, the researchers demonstrated that DD-Elo adapts more quickly to skill fluctuations without sacrificing accuracy. This method offers a backward-compatible and explainable enhancement for chess rating systems, with implementation code made publicly available for further use and development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Rating systems such as Elo serve as the gold standard for matchmaking in competitive chess. However, they inherently suffer from response lag due to their exclusive reliance on match outcomes, neglecting the granular quality of gameplay. Nevertheless, incorporating move-by-move information into rating adjustments presents a significant challenge given the substantial noise and the vastness of the game-state space. To address this, we propose the Drift-Diffusion-Enhanced Elo Rating System (DD-Elo), a novel skill assessment framework inspired by the drift diffusion model (DDM) from cognitive neuroscience. By modeling skill expression as a decision-making process, our model integrates move-level data to capture rapid skill fluctuations. We provide a rigorous mathematical derivation proving that DD-Elo maintains a bounded deviation from the traditional Elo system, ensuring theoretical alignment. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DD-Elo adapts to skill changes faster than Elo. Our findings suggest that DD-Elo offers an explainable, highly responsive, and backward-compatible solution for chess rating ecosystems. The implementation code is publicly available at https://github.com/Aquila-zhou1/DD-Elo .

items.title: Researchers propose institutional attestation as a governance model for autonomous AI systems to control high-risk actions with independent verification and tamper-evident logs [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Governing Actions, Not Agents: Institutional Attestation as a Governance Model for Autonomous AI Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a new governance model for autonomous AI systems that perform high-risk actions, such as clinical prescribing and software deployment. The model, called institutional attestation, allows AI agents to maintain autonomy in planning and reasoning but restricts their authority to execute critical actions without independent verification. Execution depends on preconditions attested by separate authoritative sources, cryptographically linked to the AI's declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy, with all decisions recorded in tamper-evident logs for independent review.

This approach formalizes how human institutions govern powerful autonomous actors by focusing on attested evidence at the point of action rather than monitoring internal reasoning. The researchers demonstrated a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrated the model's application in scenarios like software deployment and clinical prescribing, highlighting its potential to enhance safety and accountability in autonomous AI operations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26298v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autonomous AI agents may begin to perform consequential, irreversible actions such as clinical prescribing and production software deployment. This paper observes that human institutions have governed powerful autonomous actors not by monitoring their reasoning but by requiring independently attested evidence at the point of consequential action. We formalise this institutional pattern as a computational governance model for AI agent systems. Under the proposed model, an agent retains full autonomy over planning and reasoning but holds no execution authority over designated high-risk actions. Execution is conditional on preconditions that are each independently attested by a separate authoritative source, cryptographically bound to a declared intent, and evaluated by a deterministic policy. Decisions are recorded in a tamper-evident log amenable to independent re-verification. We present a proof-of-concept implementation and illustrate the model with examples from software deployment and clinical prescribing.

items.title: Researchers present COrigami, an AI pipeline generating flat-foldable, visually recognizable origami crease patterns from natural language using reinforcement learning and algorithmic optimization [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: COrigami: An AI Pipeline for Co-Designing Flat-Foldable Visually Recognisable Origami
items.summary:
Researchers have developed COrigami, an AI-driven pipeline that generates flat-foldable origami crease patterns from natural language descriptions. The system combines semantic interpretation, geometric computation, and reinforcement learning to produce crease patterns that meet strict mathematical constraints while maintaining visual recognizability. COrigami serves as a collaborative tool, providing structural designs that human artists can further refine.

The pipeline involves creating a semantic stick figure, computing base packing, solving for flat-foldability, shaping the crease pattern, and refining the model through an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. By integrating algorithmic optimization with aesthetic critique, the approach addresses the challenge of balancing physical constraints and artistic design in computational origami.

This work demonstrates how AI can support co-creativity in domains requiring multi-objective optimization, enabling reliable and mathematically grounded design assistance for physical art forms like origami.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While generative AI has achieved remarkable success in solving problems with verifiable solutions, generating physical art that satisfies both strict geometric constraints and subjective visual aesthetics remains a challenge. This paper presents an approach to tackle these difficulties in the domain of computational origami, a mathematically rigid environment that grounds artistic design within the equations of flat foldability. We present COrigami, an end-to-end AI-driven pipeline that assists the design cycle by generating crease patterns from natural language. Our pipeline involves generating a semantic stick figure, computing a base packing, solving for a flat-foldable crease pattern, shaping the flat-folded crease pattern, and refining the generated model using reinforcement learning driven by an autonomous aesthetic evaluation loop. Our system acts as a highly effective collaborative assistant, generating structural starting points that human artists can further expand and shape. By integrating algorithmic optimisation with autonomous aesthetic critique, this work demonstrates how AI systems can satisfy multi-objective physical constraints to enable reliable, mathematically grounded co-creativity.

items.title: Researchers find verifying coding agent rewards is harder than generating solutions due to underspecified intent and reward hacking, requiring co-evolving verification methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Verification Horizon: No Silver Bullet for Coding Agent Rewards
items.summary:
Researchers have found that for modern coding agents, verifying solutions is more challenging than generating them due to the inherent difficulty of capturing human intent accurately. Verification relies on proxies for intent, which are often underspecified and can lead to issues like reward hacking during model training. This shifts the traditional view that verification is easier than creation, highlighting the complexity of ensuring solutions meet intended goals.

The study evaluates verification signals based on scalability, faithfulness, and robustness, examining four types of reward mechanisms across various coding tasks. Experiments demonstrate that carefully designed verification methods can reduce reward hacking and improve task outcomes, but no single fixed reward function remains effective as agent capabilities advance. The findings emphasize the need for verification approaches to evolve alongside solution generators to maintain reliability and effectiveness.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26300v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A classical intuition holds that verifying a solution is easier than producing one. For today's coding agents, this intuition is being inverted: as foundation models develop stronger reasoning capabilities and engineering harnesses grow more sophisticated, generating complex candidate solutions is no longer difficult -- reliably verifying them has become the harder problem. Every verifier we can build is only a proxy for human intent, never the intent itself. This makes verification subject to a twofold difficulty: first, intent is underspecified by nature, making it inherently hard to faithfully check whether it has been fulfilled; second, during model training, optimization widens the gap between proxy and intent -- manifesting as reward hacking or signal saturation. To address this, we characterize the quality of verification signals along three dimensions -- scalability, faithfulness, and robustness -- and argue that achieving all three simultaneously is the central challenge. We further study four reward constructions: a test verifier for general coding tasks, a rubric verifier for frontend tasks, the user as verifier for real-world agent tasks, and an automated agent verifier for long-horizon tasks. Across different task types and policy capability levels, we conduct in-depth analysis and experiments on the core challenges of reward design and how to more effectively leverage reward signals. Experiments show that targeted verification design can effectively suppress reward hacking, improve task completion quality, and achieve significant gains across multiple internal and public benchmarks. These experiences collectively point to a core observation: no fixed reward function can remain effective as policy capability continues to grow; and verification must co-evolve with the generator.

items.title: arXiv: Empirical study evaluates tool-augmented LLM agents on 243 real-world energy market analytics tasks using live data and domain-specific tools [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How Do Tool-Augmented LLM Agents Perform on Real-World Energy Analytics Tasks?
items.summary:
A new empirical study evaluates the performance of tool-augmented large language model (LLM) agents on 243 real-world energy market analytics tasks. These tasks span market data retrieval, knowledge interpretation, and advanced quantitative modeling, requiring live data access and specialized domain knowledge. The study compares closed-source and open-source LLMs equipped with domain-specific tools such as electricity market APIs, regulatory databases, and optimization models, assessing their responses through a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol.

The evaluation environment includes expert-curated problems covering price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue estimation, hedging strategies, and optimization, with varying difficulty levels. The study highlights the interaction between model capabilities and domain tooling in a complex professional setting and publicly releases key artifacts to support reproducibility and further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26346v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic benchmarks have emerged across general-purpose and domain-specific settings, including finance, coding, law, and drug discovery, yet energy-domain evaluations remain largely limited to static knowledge recall. This is a critical gap for a sector that requires live data retrieval, specialized regulatory and market knowledge, and multi-step quantitative reasoning under real-world constraints. We present an empirical study of tool-augmented LLM agents on real-world energy market analytics tasks. Our evaluation environment includes 243 expert-curated problems across three categories: (1) Market Data Retrieval and Analysis, (2) Knowledge Retrieval and Interpretation, and (3) Advanced Quantitative Modeling and Decision Analytics. Tasks include price and demand analysis, tariff impact modeling, asset revenue and returns estimation, hedging strategy analysis, and optimization modeling, with problems spanning multiple difficulty levels. Agents are equipped with a configurable suite of domain tools, including live electricity market APIs for major U.S. ISOs, regulatory docket search, utility tariff databases, asset optimization models, and retrieval-augmented generation over energy market documents. We assess agent responses using a multi-dimensional evaluation protocol that scores approach correctness, answer accuracy, attribute alignment, and source validity, with category-aware routing to match scoring criteria to question type. We evaluate both closed-source and open-source LLMs, providing a comparative analysis of how model capability and domain tooling interact in a high-stakes professional domain. Key artifacts are publicly released to support reproducibility and future research.

items.title: arXiv paper identifies gaps in multimodal large language model evaluation, highlighting issues like temporal-spatial coherence and multimodal consistency [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: What We are Missing in Multimodal LLM Evaluation?
items.summary:
A recent paper on arXiv highlights significant gaps in the evaluation of multimodal large language models (MLLMs), which process inputs like text, images, audio, and video to generate responses. The study points out that current benchmarks focus on isolated tasks and fail to assess how well these models integrate information across different modalities. Key areas needing better evaluation include temporal-spatial coherence, understanding of the physical world, multimodal consistency, and selective attention.

The authors review existing evaluation methods and benchmark taxonomies, emphasizing that addressing these shortcomings is crucial for accurately measuring progress in multimodal intelligence. Improving evaluation frameworks will help reveal the true capabilities and limitations of MLLMs, guiding future research and development in this rapidly advancing field.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26348v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can process diverse inputs, e.g., text, images, audio, and video, and generate textual responses. While their capabilities have advanced rapidly, evaluation of such models has not kept pace. Most existing evaluation benchmarks are limited to isolated tasks and reveal little about whether a model integrates information across modalities. We examine current means for evaluating MLLMs and review the existing benchmark taxonomy to identify gaps, including temporal-spatial coherence, physical world understanding, multimodal consistency, and selective attention. Addressing these gaps is essential for measuring real progress in multimodal intelligence and exposing capability boundaries.

items.title: Researchers introduce OpenFinGym, a unified multi-task gym environment for evaluating quantitative finance agents across forecasting, trading, risk management, and fraud detection [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenFinGym: A Verifiable Multi-Task Gym Environment for Evaluating Quant Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed OpenFinGym, a unified gym environment designed to evaluate quantitative finance agents across multiple interrelated tasks including forecasting, market generation, real-time trading, and fraud detection. This platform addresses the limitations of existing tools that focus on isolated tasks, potentially overstating agent capabilities and overlooking challenges in generalization and real-market decision-making.

OpenFinGym features an automated task-construction pipeline that converts quantitative finance research into executable tasks, a containerized runtime with verification services to prevent data leakage, and a low-latency paper trading engine. It also supports long-horizon and event-driven forecasts and integrates with supervised fine-tuning and reinforcement learning methods, providing a comprehensive framework for developing and testing finance agents in realistic, multi-stage workflows.

items.title: Researchers identify compositional behavioral leakage causing cross-module interference in prompt-composed agentic systems, demonstrated on Claude Sonnet 4.6 with a new evaluation protocol [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Instruction Bleed: Cross-Module Interference in Prompt-Composed Agentic Systems
items.summary:
Researchers have identified a phenomenon called compositional behavioral leakage (CBL) in prompt-composed agentic systems, where modifying one prompt module unintentionally alters the behavior of others despite no direct dependencies. This interference arises from the architectural design of transformers, which lack formal boundaries between concatenated modules. The team demonstrated CBL on the Claude Sonnet 4.6 agent using a novel three-channel evaluation protocol that perturbs non-focal modules by volume, content, and form, finding that only content changes produced measurable effects without flipping recommendations, indicating subtle but cumulative impacts on agent decisions.

The study distinguishes CBL from other known failure modes such as adversarial attacks or privacy leaks and provides an operational definition, a reusable testing protocol, and a set of falsifiable predictions. These contributions establish cross-module interference measurement as an essential component for evaluating prompt-composed agents, highlighting the need for more rigorous assessment methods to ensure reliable agent behavior in complex modular systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26356v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practitioners of prompt-composed agentic systems report a recurring failure mode: editing one prompt module silently shifts the behavior of others despite no shared variable or executable dependency. We formalize this as compositional behavioral leakage (CBL): interference between modules sharing a context window. CBL is enabled by architectural non-isolation: transformer self-attention provides no formal boundary between concatenated modules. We probe CBL on a deployed job-evaluation agent (Claude Sonnet 4.6, 144 trials) through a reusable three-channel protocol that perturbs non-focal modules along volume, content, and form. Only the content channel produces a detectable paired effect (Cohen's d = 0.63, bootstrap 95% CI excluding zero); no recommendation flipped -- a sub-threshold regime invisible to standard QA but compounding across the thousands of decisions a deployed agent makes. CBL is orthogonal to known agent-failure axes (adversarial injection, cognitive degradation, multi-agent fault propagation, privacy leakage). We contribute an operational definition, a reusable protocol, a falsifiable prediction set, and a system-class characterization, establishing cross-module interference measurement as a requirement for prompt-composed agent evaluation.

items.title: arXiv paper presents a mathematical interpretation of Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis and proposes the Qualitative Engine for Science to address limits in AI-driven scientific discovery [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Accelerating Returns and the Qualitative Engine for Science
items.summary:
A new paper on arXiv offers a mathematical interpretation of Ray Kurzweil's accelerating returns thesis, which suggests that technological progress in fields like computing, AI, brain science, and biotechnology is self-reinforcing and exponential. The paper argues that while this acceleration enhances executional and infrastructural capabilities, it does not fully address the core challenge of scientific discovery, which requires qualitative reasoning to identify when existing frameworks are inadequate and to determine the next conceptual steps.

The authors highlight recent AI benchmark results showing a significant gap between human flexible reasoning and current AI performance, emphasizing the need for systems that support qualitative scientific insight. They propose the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) as a tool to complement accelerating quantitative capabilities by preserving and organizing the human wisdom involved in scientific discovery. This approach underscores that the value of such tools extends beyond the timeline for achieving artificial general intelligence, focusing instead on sustaining meaningful human understanding in science.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26359v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ray Kurzweil described a thesis of accelerating returns, which is the most influential narratives in discussions of technological progress. Its central claim is that advances in multiple technological fields, especially compute, artificial intelligence, brain science, and biotechnology, interact in such a way that progress becomes self-amplifying and approximately exponential. This paper gives a simple mathematical interpretation of that claim and then argues that, even if such acceleration is real, it does not by itself resolve the central problem of scientific discovery. The reason is that accelerating returns apply most naturally to executional and infrastructural capability, whereas genuine discovery often depends on a different capacity: qualitative reasoning about when a current framework is structurally inadequate and what conceptual move is needed next. Recent ARC-AGI-3 results sharpen this distinction: humans solve the benchmark at ceiling, whereas frontier AI systems remain below 1%, indicating that the gap between current AI and human flexible reasoning is still very large. At the same time, Demis Hassabis has emphasized that humans must retain their sense of meaning and what they choose to focus their lives on, a reminder that the future of AI is not only a technical forecast but also a question of what forms of human understanding are worth preserving and transmitting. This paper positions the Qualitative Engine for Science (QES) [3] as a response to that missing capacity. In this view, the Kurzweil theory helps explain why quantitative capability may accelerate, while QES addresses the central problem in scientific discovery that acceleration alone does not solve. Its value does not depend on when AGI arrives, but on the fact that the processes of scientific discovery themselves constitute a form of human wisdom worth preserving, organizing, and making accessible.

items.title: Researchers introduce Narration-of-Thought, a system prompt that improves ethical reasoning in large language models by reducing stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression without additional training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Narration-of-Thought: Inference-Time Scaffolding for Defeasible Ethical Reasoning in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Narration-of-Thought (NoT), a system prompt designed to enhance ethical reasoning in large language models by addressing two common issues: stakeholder collapse and uncertainty suppression. NoT structures the reasoning process into five distinct sections—protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, and commitment—without requiring additional training or fine-tuning. Testing on 100 moral dilemma scenarios across multiple models showed that NoT significantly reduces stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to between 1% and 24%.

The study demonstrated that NoT's improvements are not due to increased token usage but stem from its structured approach, with each section contributing to better ethical reasoning. Further enhancements were achieved through textual-gradient descent, and a multi-stakeholder debate protocol using NoT led to near-complete consensus in ethical judgments. This method provides transparent reasoning traces that clarify stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainties, offering a reliable foundation for deploying ethical AI agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26366v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Standard chain-of-thought on moral dilemmas exhibits two failure modes: stakeholder collapse (the trace names at most one party with a stake in the outcome) and uncertainty suppression (no explicit unknowns or hedges before committing to an action). We introduce narration-of-thought (NoT), a system prompt that structures chain-of-thought into five sections: protagonist, stakeholders, two-step consequences, uncertainty, then commitment. NoT adds no training, parameters, or fine-tuning. On 100 DailyDilemmas scenarios across four generators from three vendors, NoT cuts stakeholder collapse from up to 31% to under 1% and uncertainty suppression from up to 72% to 1-24% on every model. A matched-budget verbose-CoT control rules out token spend as the active ingredient; NoT retains Cliff's delta advantages of +0.79 to +0.90 on stakeholder count and +0.65 to +0.93 on uncertainty score for three of four generators, and a section ablation attributes each shift to its specific sub-instruction. Textual-gradient descent initialised at NoT improves the scaffold further; a cross-family training judge (different vendor from the generator) dominates an in-family one on every measured axis. Extended to a five-round multi-stakeholder debate protocol, the scaffold converts a 6% standoff into 95% full consensus on a calibration set and 100% combined convergence on a DailyDilemmas replication. The resulting traces externalise the stakeholders, consequences, and uncertainty grounding each commitment, providing an auditable substrate for dependable agentic deployment.

items.title: Researchers propose Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search to solve extremal combinatorial geometry problems, achieving new best-known results on five of six tested problems including Max-N3IL and Smallest Complete Set [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometry-Aware MCTS for Extremal Problems in Combinatorial Geometry
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework to address extremal problems in combinatorial geometry involving point configurations on an $n \times n$ grid with strict geometric constraints. This approach improves upon classical solvers and standard machine learning models by incrementally updating feasible actions and enforcing constraints more efficiently, notably reducing complexity in problems like the No-Three-in-Line (Max-N3IL). The method also leverages geometric symmetries to enhance search efficiency.

Extensive experiments demonstrate that this framework achieves new best-known results on five out of six tested problems, including finding larger configurations for Max-N3IL and tighter upper bounds for the Smallest Complete Set problem. These findings establish Geometry-Aware MCTS as a versatile tool for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26399v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study certain extremal problems in combinatorial geometry that ask about configurations of points in an $n \times n$ grid that satisfy strict, global geometric constraints. Classical exact solvers suffer from combinatorial explosion for these types of problems, and standard reinforcement learning and transformer-based models struggle with the sparse reward "validity cliff" and quadratic token-consumption limits. To overcome these bottlenecks, we propose a Geometry-Aware Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) framework. Our approach strictly enforces geometric constraints through incremental updates to the feasible action space. For constraints about collections of collinear points, like those that occur in the classic No-Three-in-Line problem (Max-N3IL), this mechanism reduces the constraint checking complexity from $O(n^3)$ to $O(n^2)$. To improve search efficiency, we exploit geometric symmetries in two ways: canonical pruning during node expansion to reduce the branching factor, and symmetric batch transitions to accelerate the discovery of promising configurations. We perform extensive experiments and establish new best-known computational results on five out of six of the problems that we considered. Notably, for Max-N3IL we find configurations of size roughly $1.8 n$ for grids of size $82 \le n \le 119$. For the Smallest Complete Set problem, we find configurations of size roughly $0.95 n$, providing new upper bounds within the tested grids. This work establishes Geometry-Aware MCTS as a highly adaptable framework for discovering novel configurations in combinatorial geometry.

items.title: Researchers propose an agentic aggregator framework for electric bus fleet operations integrating scheduling optimization and supervisory agents to manage pricing, disturbances, and vehicle-to-grid flexibility [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: When Agents Meet Electric Bus Fleet Operations: Pricing Behavior, Trade-offs, and Policy Implications in an Aggregator Framework
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an agentic aggregator framework to enhance the operation of electric bus fleets by integrating an optimization-based scheduling model with supervisory agents that manage disturbances, pricing adaptations, and schedule evaluations. This framework coordinates complex factors such as service reliability, battery charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) interactions to maintain feasible schedules and improve flexibility use.

A case study of a realistic depot scenario tested the framework's performance under various conditions, including service delays, energy deviations, and price shocks, using both profit-based and operation-based coordination modes. The results demonstrated that the agentic system can selectively trigger real-time re-optimization and support adaptive fleet-grid coordination, though it also highlighted a trade-off where profit-oriented configurations might extract value from public transport operators.

These findings suggest that while agentic aggregators offer promising tools for managing electric bus V2G operations, their implementation in public fleet contexts requires transparent coordination, auditable pricing mechanisms, and clear value-sharing policies to ensure equitable and effective deployment.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26400v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agentic systems are changing how complex operational tasks are coordinated, introducing a new paradigm for connecting heterogeneous data sources and automating processes. Electric bus fleets provide a relevant test case. Their operation requires continuous coordination between service reliability, battery state-of-charge, charger availability, electricity prices, route-energy uncertainty, and vehicle-to-grid (V2G) opportunities. This paper proposes an agentic aggregator framework that streamlines this decision environment by coupling an optimization-based electric bus scheduling model with supervisory agents for disturbance detection, tariff adaptation, and schedule evaluation. The optimization core enforces physical feasibility across routes, chargers, batteries, and V2G exchanges, while the agentic layer interprets changing operating conditions, triggers real-time re-optimization when needed, and defines how flexibility value is allocated between the aggregator and the public transport operator (PTO). A realistic depot case study evaluates day-ahead and real-time operations under profit-based and operation-based coordination modes, considering service delays, route-energy deviations, electricity price shocks, and combined disturbances. The results show that agentic aggregation can support adaptive fleet-grid coordination by maintaining feasible schedules, activating re-optimization selectively, and improving the use of charging and V2G flexibility. However, they also reveal a critical trade-off: the same agentic capability that reduces operational complexity can extract value from the PTO when configured around profit-oriented pricing. These findings suggest that agentic aggregators can become useful for managing electric bus V2G operations, but their deployment in public-fleet contexts requires transparent coordination modes, auditable tariff-setting, and explicit value-sharing rules.

items.title: Researchers propose a lattice-theoretic method to create unbiased, self-consistent set-valued oracles for AI probability estimates, addressing self-reference problems in future event prediction [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Unbiased Canonical Set-Valued Oracles Via Lattice Theory
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a lattice-theoretic approach to address the self-reference problem faced by non-agentic "oracle" AI systems that estimate probabilities of future events. These systems can alter the probabilities they predict once their answers are known and acted upon. Instead of providing a single probability, the proposed method outputs a credal set that is unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned, using the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem to identify a canonical, nontrivial solution.

The approach ensures existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness of the solution and reduces to classical point estimates for non-performative questions. For binary events, the canonical answer forms an interval under certain assumptions. This lattice-theoretic framework generalizes from binary events to arbitrary random variables, replacing conditional probabilities with conditional laws. The study concludes with open questions about the broader applicability of the interval characterization in this generalized setting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26418v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A non-agentic "oracle" AI that estimates probabilities of future events faces a self-reference problem: once its answer is learned and acted upon, it can change the very probability it was asked to report. One response, advocated for the Scientist AI programme, is to ask only counterfactual questions, evaluated as if the answer had no influence. We observe that such answers tend to become irrelevant the moment they are learned, precisely because their premise is then false. We therefore explore a self-referential alternative in which the oracle reports not a single probability but a credal set that is simultaneously unbiased and self-consistent with the consequences of being learned. The naive self-consistency requirement is satisfied by too many sets (including the useless answer $[0,1]$), so the problem is to single out a canonical, nontrivial member. We do so with the Knaster--Tarski fixed-point theorem on the complete lattice of closed credal sets, taking the least fixed point of a suitably defined isotone operator; a variant instead reports the least fixed point that contains every self-consistent point estimate. We prove existence, self-consistency, and nonemptiness, show that the construction collapses to the classical point answer for non-performative questions, and that for a binary event the canonical answer is, under a natural hull-factoring assumption, an interval. The development is purely lattice-theoretic and extends unchanged from a binary event $B$ to an arbitrary random variable $X$, with $P(B\mid A,C)$ replaced by the conditional law $\mathcal{L}(X\mid A,C)$. We close with open questions, including whether the interval characterization itself survives that generalization.

items.title: Researchers evaluate confidence interval methods for classifier performance metrics in text classification with small samples and nested data, proposing improved approaches for large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Estimating Uncertainty in Classifier Performance with Applications to Large Language Models and Nested Data
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated various confidence interval methods for classifier performance metrics in text classification, particularly under conditions common in social science research such as small sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and nested data structures. They found that commonly used methods like the Wald interval and basic percentile bootstrap often provide inaccurate uncertainty estimates, especially when datasets are small or classifier performance is high. The study highlights improved accuracy using methods such as Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap, especially for F1 score calculations.

The research also addresses the challenge of texts nested within individuals, demonstrating that adjustments for effective sample size and degrees of freedom are necessary for accurate interval estimation. Among bootstrap approaches, the hierarchical bootstrap performs better than the cluster bootstrap when individuals contribute a moderate number of texts but tends to be overly conservative with fewer texts per individual. By offering guidance on appropriate confidence interval estimation, the study aims to enhance transparency in machine learning applications and encourage careful consideration of validation sample sizes during study design.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26422v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Researchers increasingly use text classification--supervised models or large language models--to measure constructs from natural language, providing metrics such as recall and precision as evidence of their validity. Yet, though these metrics are point estimates subject to sampling variation, measures of uncertainty are inconsistently reported alongside them. Further, when they are reported, they are often estimated with methods that are not appropriate when relevant labelled datasets are small or performance is high. To increase and improve confidence interval reporting in the field, this paper evaluates confidence interval methods for performance metrics under conditions typical of social science text classification: small to moderate sample sizes, infrequent constructs, and texts nested within individuals. Accuracy is improved with the use of Agresti-Coull, Wilson, Clopper-Pearson, and a novel pseudo-count regularized bootstrap (which is particularly relevant to the calculation of F1). When texts are nested within individuals, we demonstrate that adjustment for both effective N and the appropriate degrees of freedom is necessary for producing accurate analytic intervals. Among bootstrap intervals, the hierarchical bootstrap is more accurate than the cluster bootstrap when individuals produce a moderate number of texts but overly conservative when individuals produce only a few. By providing guidance to the field on appropriate interval estimation, we aim to improve the transparency of machine learning applications, and to encourage greater attention to the validation sample size at the design stage.

items.title: Researchers show supervised machine learning cannot achieve symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning due to data and training limitations, with experiments on Euler Net and GPT-5 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data-driven Machine Learning Cannot Reach Symbolic-level Logical Reasoning -- The Limit of the Scaling Law
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that supervised machine learning systems face fundamental limitations in achieving symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning, even with increased training data and time. Their study identifies two key methodological barriers: training data cannot differentiate all 24 valid types of syllogistic reasoning, and the end-to-end learning approach creates conflicting objectives between pattern recognition and logical reasoning components. Experimental results show that models like Euler Net fail to perform rigorous syllogistic reasoning, and while advanced models such as GPT-5 can reach high accuracy on certain reasoning tasks, they may still produce incorrect explanations.

The research further reveals that the form of input—whether words, repeated words, simple symbols, or random symbols—significantly affects reasoning performance. Despite achieving apparent accuracy, supervised learning models stop training early and do not attain the strict logical rigor characteristic of symbolic reasoning. These findings suggest inherent constraints in data-driven machine learning approaches for complex logical tasks, highlighting a gap between current AI capabilities and true symbolic reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Sphere neural networks have achieved symbolic level syllogistic reasoning without training data, raising the question of where the limit of the scaling law for logical reasoning lies, i.e., whether data-driven machine learning systems can achieve the same level by increasing training data and training time. We show two methodological limitations that prevent supervised deep learning from reaching the symbolic-level syllogistic reasoning: (1) training data can not distinguish all 24 types of valid syllogistic reasoning; (2) end-to-end mapping from premises to conclusion introduces contradictory training targets between neural components for pattern recognition and logical reasoning. Beside theoretical analysis, we experimentally illustrate that Euler Net cannot achieve rigorous syllogistic reasoning. We further challenge the most recent ChatGPTs (GPT-5-nano and GPT-5) to determine the satisfiability of syllogistic statements in four surface forms (patterns): words, double words, simple symbols, and long random symbols, showing that surface forms affect the reasoning performance and that ChatGPT GPT-5 may reach 100% accuracy but still provide incorrect explanations. As empirical training processes are stopped after achieving 100% accuracy, we conclude that supervised machine learning systems will not attain the rigour of symbolic logical reasoning.

items.title: Researchers introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark for evaluating retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph-augmented generation using general and medical datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: MKG-RAG-Bench: Benchmarking Retrieval in Multimodal Knowledge Graph-Augmented Generation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced MKG-RAG-Bench, a new cross-domain benchmark designed to evaluate retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph-augmented generation (MKG-RAG). This benchmark addresses the challenges of retrieving heterogeneous and multimodal knowledge, which is critical for grounding large language models but often overlooked by existing benchmarks. MKG-RAG-Bench includes datasets from general and medical domains with aligned question-answering tasks to assess both retrieval and downstream generation performance.

The benchmark was developed using a large language model-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge and generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision. Experiments across various retriever types and modality settings demonstrate that effective multimodal retrieval remains a significant challenge and strongly influences the quality of generated outputs. By focusing on retrieval as a primary evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing the development of MKG-RAG systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26458v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) over knowledge graphs has emerged as a promising approach for grounding large language models, yet existing benchmarks largely overlook the challenges of retrieval in multimodal knowledge graph RAG (MKG-RAG). In practice, retrieval is a critical bottleneck: multimodal knowledge is heterogeneous, difficult to align across modalities, and often poorly served by retrievers designed for unstructured corpora. To address this gap, we introduce MKG-RAG-Bench, a cross-domain benchmark explicitly designed to evaluate retrieval in MKG-RAG. MKG-RAG-Bench is constructed from two multimodal knowledge graphs spanning general and medical domains, and includes carefully aligned question-answering datasets that support controlled evaluation of both retrieval and downstream generation. The benchmark is built using an LLM-based curation pipeline that filters low-utility knowledge, generates structurally grounded queries with exact supervision, and systematically covers diverse modality configurations. Through extensive experiments across representative retriever families and modality settings, we show that effective multimodal retrieval remains challenging yet crucial for end-to-end MKG-RAG performance, and that retrieval quality strongly determines generation outcomes. By isolating retrieval as a first-class evaluation target, MKG-RAG-Bench provides a principled foundation for diagnosing current limitations and advancing multimodal knowledge graph RAG systems.

items.title: Researchers present auto-psych, an agent-based system automating theory discovery and experimentation in computational cognitive science using crowdsourced human data [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: auto-psych: Automating the science of mind using agent-driven theory discovery and experimentation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed auto-psych, an agent-based system that automates theory discovery and experimentation in computational cognitive science by independently collecting human data through crowdsourced surveys. The system uses nested loops where one generates and critiques cognitive models while the other designs and conducts experiments online, enabling rapid and reliable theory testing. Tested on a classic cognitive psychology problem involving perceptions of randomness in coin flip sequences, auto-psych produced theories that fit human data better than existing scientific models.

The system's design allows it to recover known theories from synthetic data and improve upon them through systematic experimentation. By leveraging crowdsourcing platforms for scalable data collection and representing theories as code, auto-psych demonstrates the potential for AI-driven automation in psychological research. This approach could accelerate scientific discovery by integrating hypothesis generation, experimental design, data collection, and analysis into a unified automated workflow.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26460v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI-based scientific automation is increasingly possible by using agents to generate hypotheses, design experiments, and analyze data. Data collection is a major bottleneck in this pipeline, however. Psychology, and computational cognitive science in particular, is well-positioned to benefit from AI experimentation because theories are often represented as code and crowdsourcing platforms enable programmatic human data collection at scale. Here, we apply automated discovery techniques to the project of generating theories in computational cognitive science, with an agent-based system collecting human data independently through crowdsourced survey experiments. As a testbed, we use a classic case study from cognitive psychology: judging which sequences of coin flips seem subjectively more random. Our system, auto-psych, uses nested agent-based discovery loops to generate explanatory theories of human behavior. The inner loop conjectures, fits, and critiques probabilistic cognitive models; the outer loop designs experiments to test these models, launches them online, and analyzes the data. This system can quickly and reliably recover ground-truth theories from synthetic data via systematic experimentation, but the nested structure is critical to model performance. Further, in three independent sequences of human experiments, the system finds theories that fit the data better than theories generated from the scientific literature. This work thus demonstrates the feasibility of automated data collection and theory discovery in computational cognitive science.

items.title: Researchers find large reasoning models spend more time on incorrect problems while humans spend less, revealing opposite deliberation allocation despite similar difficulty tracking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Humans Disengage, Reasoning Models Persist: Separating Difficulty Registration from Deliberation Allocation
items.summary:
Researchers have found that large reasoning models (LRMs) and humans exhibit opposite patterns in how they allocate time when solving problems. While both spend more time on harder problems overall, LRMs tend to spend more time on problems they answer incorrectly, whereas humans spend less time on their incorrect attempts. This study distinguishes between two aspects of deliberation: how response time correlates with difficulty across different problems and how time is allocated between successes and failures on the same problem.

The analysis, conducted on a dataset comparing human and LRM performance, shows that although both humans and LRMs similarly track problem difficulty across items, they differ significantly in their within-item time allocation. Humans appear to disengage from problems they expect to fail, while LRMs continue deliberating longer when uncertain, which often leads to failure. This divergence suggests that LRMs and humans use different stopping policies despite sharing a common difficulty signal, highlighting contrasting approaches to problem-solving and metareasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26502v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large reasoning models (LRMs) take longer on harder problems, just as humans do. This surface similarity hides an opposite pattern within items. When an LRM gets a problem wrong, it spends more tokens than when it gets the same problem right; humans do the reverse, spending less time on the trials they get wrong. We separate two levels of deliberation: how response time tracks difficulty across items (registration), and, with item identity held fixed, whether an agent spends more on its own failures or successes (allocation). On a public matched human-LRM corpus, humans and all five thinking LRMs reproduce the known cross-item alignment (registration) but diverge within items (allocation): every LRM shows a large wrong-vs-right effect (Cohen's d = 1.47-3.13 on H-ARC) while humans show the opposite sign. The comparison stays inside each agent's own scale; we never put seconds and tokens on one axis. The dissociation holds under item fixed effects, replicates across datasets, and is absent in a non-thinking baseline. We read the human pattern as engagement versus abandonment: people stay on items they expect to solve and give up on the rest. We read the LRM pattern as length driven by uncertainty: chains grow when the model is unsure, which is exactly when it tends to fail. Both policies produce the same cross-item correlation with difficulty, so they look aligned on the measure prior work has used; the divergence shows up only once item identity is fixed. Under resource-rational metareasoning, the split is between two stopping policies that share a difficulty signal but implement opposite control; trace length captures the signal and misses the control.

items.title: arXiv: NeuraDock releases open-source EEG agent tutorial for real-time visual cognitive load analysis using quality-gated Alpha dynamics workflow [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: NeuraDock Visual Cognitive Load Agent Tutorial: A Quality-Gated Open-Source EEG Workflow for Alpha Dynamics and Real-Time Applications
items.summary:
NeuraDock has released an open-source EEG agent tutorial that guides users through a quality-gated workflow for analyzing Alpha dynamics and visual cognitive load in real time. The tutorial enables researchers and developers to install the agent, perform EEG preprocessing and quality control, generate Alpha activity figures, compare cognitive load between rest and task conditions, and utilize a real-time API with an interpretation layer for quality risk assessment. This approach bridges the gap between offline EEG analysis and real-time cognitive load monitoring by integrating acquisition, custom quality control, feature extraction, and web API components.

The tutorial includes validation using a public mini-dataset, where the agent processed 18 recordings and produced within-subject comparisons showing task-related posterior Alpha suppression in most cases. It also benchmarks online API latency and demonstrates initial evidence of repeatability in cognitive load measures. Designed for applied teams, the tutorial offers a transparent and reproducible path from raw EEG data to real-time visual cognitive load prototypes.

items.title: Researchers present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture combining a deterministic EEG engine with a hardware-aware language layer for low-channel EEG analysis and boundary-aware context grounding [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Boundary-Aware Context Grounding for A Low-Channel EEG Agent
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NeuraDock Agent, an open-source system designed to improve low-channel electroencephalography (EEG) analysis by combining a deterministic local EEG processing engine with a hardware-aware language model layer. This architecture ensures that the language model receives only curated, context-specific summaries about the EEG hardware, workflows, and scientific boundaries, while raw data remains local. The system aims to prevent unsupported interpretations common in sparse EEG data by grounding analysis within known hardware and implementation limits.

The NeuraDock Agent was evaluated through multiple tests, including repeated numerical analyses of EEG recordings, robustness checks under data transmission failures, and boundary-awareness benchmarks involving various question types and language models. These evaluations demonstrated consistent results and effective handling of data boundaries, supporting the approach as a practical method for calibrating EEG data interpretation. However, the researchers note that these findings do not establish clinical validity or a definitive cognitive-load index.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26519v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) can make scientific software easier to use. However, a general model does not automatically know which measurements a particular sensor can support, which algorithms are implemented in the current software, or which conclusions are justified by a computed result. These distinctions are especially important for low-channel electroencephalography (EEG), where sparse spatial coverage and variable signal quality make plausible but unsupported interpretations easy to produce. We present NeuraDock Agent, an open-source architecture that separates a deterministic local EEG engine from a hardware-aware language layer. The numerical engine parses recordings, performs quality control, executes reviewed spectral workflows, and writes machine-readable artifacts. The LLM receives only a compact, allowlisted summary and a versioned context pack. The context describes the seven-channel hardware, reviewed workflows, result fields, implementation boundaries, scientific limits, and reference cases. Raw EEG and dense per-sample arrays remain local We evaluate the system at three levels. First, 12 recordings produced identical structured results over ten numerical repetitions, and a complete Rest/Task run produced identical result, report, and figure hashes over three repetitions. Second, request-capture and failure-injection experiments confirmed the tested data boundary and preservation of local artifacts under HTTP, malformed-output, and connection failures. Third, a boundary-awareness benchmark tested 36 ordinary and adversarial questions under four context ablations and two LLMs, yielding 288 outputs.These results support hardware- and implementation-aware grounding as a practical mechanism for calibrating what an EEG agent accepts, qualifies, or refuses; they do not establish clinical validity or a validated absolute cognitive-load index.

items.title: Researchers develop a framework for radical AI interpretability to infer AI systems' beliefs and desires from computational data, addressing safety and trust challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Radical AI Interpretability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new framework for interpreting AI systems as agents by combining the philosophical approach of radical interpretation with mechanistic interpretability techniques. This framework aims to determine an AI system's beliefs, desires, and meanings based on its computational data, addressing critical safety concerns such as understanding AI goals and detecting deception. The work proposes criteria for evaluating interpretability tools and emphasizes that beliefs and desires must be assessed holistically rather than piecemeal to avoid distortions.

The framework highlights that AI systems may not share human concepts, making interpretation challenging but also providing constraints that help in attributing attitudes and propositional structures. By jointly analyzing these elements, the approach offers a more reliable method for reading AI internals, which is essential for building trust and ensuring the safe deployment of AI technologies.
