items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26918v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models can serve as capable long-horizon agents, but their out-of-distribution (OOD) generalization remains weak. We identify a key source of this failure as task insensitivity: when faced with similar but distinct tasks, models might apply patterns learned during training and fail to solve the task at hand. We show that models often continue with actions aligned with the original task even when the instruction is semantically corrupted and cannot be directly answered. We further find that, when we replace the task description in a trained prompt with another similar but distinct task, the model may still output the same action. This behavior is accompanied by a consistent training-time attention drift away from task tokens and toward local observations, suggesting an optimization bias toward shortcuts. To mitigate this problem, we propose Task-Perturbed NLL Optimization, a lightweight contrastive regularizer that explicitly encourages action dependence on the task instruction. Extensive evaluations show that our intervention improves task sensitivity and OOD generalization while preserving more stable attention to task tokens.

items.title: Researchers analyze chain-of-thought training in large language model agents, finding improvements mainly in prompt action prediction and out-of-domain generalization through selective supervision masking [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Do CoT Training Gains Land in LLM based Agents?
items.summary:
Researchers have investigated the effects of chain-of-thought (CoT) training on large language model agents, focusing on whether improvements come from enhanced reasoning during action generation or better direct action prediction from prompts. Their study found that while CoT reasoning does not significantly increase the advantage of reasoning-based actions over prompt-based actions, CoT training notably improves the quality of prompt action predictions. Additionally, models at later training stages tend to rely more on prompt information rather than revising actions based on CoT reasoning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26935v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is widely used in language-model agents, but prior work has shown that verbalized CoT is not always faithful and may instead reflect post-hoc reasoning, which means the model already knows the answer before reasoning. We therefore ask what CoT training is actually improving: is the model getting better at changing its action through generated reasoning, or is it getting better at predicting the action directly from the prompt? We study this question by comparing \emph{prompt actions} (predicting action without CoT) with CoT actions (predicting action with CoT). Across checkpoints, prompt-action quality improves substantially. While interacting with the environment, the relative advantage of CoT actions over prompt actions remains similar, showing that CoT training does not widen the advantage of CoT reasoning, and it helps to improve the quality of prompt actions. We further find that later checkpoints are less likely to revise the action in response to CoT, suggesting greater reliance on the prompt. Motivated by these patterns, we selectively mask action-token supervision on a fraction of training examples. This intervention improves out-of-domain generalization.

items.title: Researchers propose Look-Before-Move framework for narrative-grounded visual attention and camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, introducing a new benchmark with 50 stories and 1585 shots [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Look-Before-Move: Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention in Dynamic 3D Story Worlds
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Look-Before-Move framework to enhance camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds by enabling narrative-grounded visual attention. This approach allows the camera to actively decide what to observe and how to move smoothly while adhering to narrative intent and physical constraints. The framework separates observation specification from motion execution through a Semantic Observation Contract, Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search, and Semantic Trajectory Grounding, improving subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality compared to existing methods.

To support this research, the team developed a new dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, which includes 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots featuring animated characters and semantic scene configurations. Experiments demonstrate the framework's effectiveness in organizing visual attention before generating camera motion, highlighting its potential for advancing embodied AI and world models in complex 3D environments.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26964v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As embodied AI and world models increasingly operate in dynamic 3D environments, visual perception must move beyond passively interpreting given observations toward actively deciding what to observe. We study this problem through camera planning in dynamic 3D story worlds, where the camera must not only generate smooth motion, but also decide what visual evidence should be acquired before it moves. We formulate this capability as Narrative-Grounded World Visual Attention, where the camera acts as an embodied observer that determines what to observe, how to compose the observation, and how to shift attention over time under narrative intent and physical 3D constraints. To realize this capability, we propose Look-Before-Move, a camera planning framework that separates observation specification from motion execution. It first builds a Semantic Observation Contract to convert directorial intent into executable visual constraints, then performs Monte Carlo Viewpoint Search to find narrative-compliant and geometrically feasible viewpoints, and finally applies Semantic Trajectory Grounding to connect selected viewpoints into continuous, collision-aware, and temporally coherent camera motion. We further construct a dynamic 3D Story World Benchmark based on StoryBlender, covering 50 stories, 457 scenes, and 1585 shots with animated characters, semantic scene configurations, and executable 3D environments. Experiments show that our framework improves subject perception, intent consistency, and trajectory quality over representative baselines, demonstrating the importance of organizing visual attention before generating camera motion.

items.title: arXiv: Einstein World Models propose integrating visual-temporal rollouts into LLM reasoning to enhance complex thought beyond text-based methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Einstein World Models
items.summary:
Researchers propose Einstein World Models (EWMs), a new framework that integrates visual-temporal rollouts into large language model (LLM) reasoning processes to enhance complex thought beyond text alone. EWMs enable LLMs to generate and inspect short visual simulations of scenarios as hypotheses, supporting reasoning in ways that purely textual methods may not achieve. This approach extends the concept of tool use in LLMs, such as web search or code execution, into the realm of visual thought experiments.

The framework involves an LLM calling a specialized world-module to produce these visual rollouts, which are then incorporated into the reasoning trace rather than treated as final answers. By combining language with visual counterfactual reasoning, EWMs aim to improve the ability of AI systems to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience, potentially advancing the capabilities of artificial intelligence in complex problem-solving.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26969v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Does intelligence require the ability to reason about phenomena beyond direct experience? It is natural to suspect that some complex thought cannot be captured through language alone. However, of particular concern to this work, is whether visualising counterfactual events can complement language as a mechanism for complex thought. We ask whether LLMs can be trained to utilise such visualisation mechanisms, in a way that benefits their reasoning abilities. Motivated by this question, we propose Einstein World Models. EWMs are a blueprint for LLM-based reasoning systems that place visual-temporal rollouts inside the reasoning trace, allowing them to reason in ways that text alone may not support well. In an EWM, the LLM calls a world-module (not to be confused with a world model), to produce short rollouts of scenes under consideration. The returned rollout is treated not as the answer, but as an inspectable hypothesis that can support later reasoning. Einstein World Models extend the capability of LLMs for tool calling (such as web search or code execution), into the domain of visual thought experiments.

items.title: arXiv: Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework AURORA-AI improves resilience and fairness in AI systems under dynamic conditions, outperforming established controllers in simulations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Adaptive Utility driven Resource Orchestration for Resilient AI (AURORA-AI)
items.summary:
AURORA-AI is a new adaptive resource orchestration framework designed to enhance the resilience and fairness of AI systems operating under dynamic and non-stationary conditions. It integrates advanced control methods and fairness-aware utility metrics to continuously allocate computational resources across diverse AI models, optimizing overall performance, fairness, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability. Evaluated through simulations involving demographic bias shocks, concept drift, and unexpected disruptions, AURORA-AI outperformed several established controllers by achieving faster recovery, improving key performance quantiles, reducing demographic parity gaps, and maintaining system stability.

The framework's closed-loop policy combines Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control with Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, enabling it to adapt resource distribution in real time to maximize a composite utility function. Compared to static and reinforcement learning-based controllers, AURORA-AI demonstrated immediate recovery from severe disruptions and enhanced fairness metrics, indicating its potential for practical deployment in human-centric AI applications.

These results suggest that incorporating fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory offers a promising approach to maintaining resilient and equitable AI systems amid changing operational environments and unexpected challenges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27005v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Modern AI systems are increasingly deployed under non-stationary computational, demographic, and operational conditions in which static resource allocation strategies degrade both predictive performance and human-centric properties such as fairness and explainability. This paper presents AURORA-AI, an Adaptive Utility-driven Resource Orchestration framework for Resilient AI that unifies Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman feedback control, Lyapunov-based stability monitoring, and a fairness-aware composite utility into a single closed-loop policy.The framework continuously redistributes computational budget across a population of heterogeneous AI models so that the global utility, defined jointly over predictive performance, demographic parity, cost, latency, robustness, and interpretability, remains maximised under disruption. The framework is evaluated in a stress-rich discrete-time simulation that concurrently injects demographic bias shocks, gradual concept drift, and abrupt black-swan disruptions, and is compared against five established controllers including Static, Round Robin, Greedy, LinUCB, and a deep reinforcement-learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimisation. AURORA-AI achieves immediate recovery from the black-swan event compared to eighty-eight time steps for the Static baseline and twenty-two for Proximal Policy Optimisation, lifts the alpha-quantile and the super-quantile by twenty-nine and twenty-five percent respectively, simultaneously reduces the mean and maximum demographic parity gap, and increases the fraction of Lyapunov-stable operating steps. These results indicate that fairness-aware adaptive orchestration grounded in stability theory is a practical and theoretically motivated path toward resilient human-centric AI deployment.

items.title: Researchers propose semantic early-stopping for iterative LLM agent loops to reduce token use by 38% without quality loss, validated on multi-hop question answering tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Semantic Early-Stopping for Iterative LLM Agent Loops
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a semantic early-stopping method for iterative loops in multi-agent large language models (LLMs), such as a Writer and Critic system, to reduce token usage without sacrificing answer quality. Unlike traditional fixed iteration caps that stop processing after a set number of steps regardless of progress, this approach halts the loop when consecutive draft embeddings show minimal semantic change and the answer quality plateaus. This method was validated on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering tasks, achieving a 38% reduction in token use while maintaining comparable answer quality.

The study provides a theoretical foundation proving deterministic termination and well-definedness of the stopping criterion, supported by machine-checked claims. It also introduces an efficient evaluation protocol that replays stopping policies over identical draft trajectories and caches judge calls to enable low-cost, paired comparisons of efficiency versus quality. Empirical results on the HotpotQA dataset demonstrate that a judge-free semantic stopper effectively reduces operational tokens, whereas a quality-gated variant that judges each round incurs higher costs. The findings suggest that the challenge lies more in selecting the best iteration rather than deciding when to stop.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27009v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-agent large language model (LLM) loops, for example a Writer that drafts and a Critic that revises, are almost always terminated by a fixed iteration cap (max_iterations). This is a syntactic kill-switch: it is blind to whether the answer is still improving, so it over-spends tokens on easy inputs and truncates hard ones. We study semantic early-stopping: the loop halts when consecutive draft embeddings stop changing in meaning (cosine distance with a patience window) and the answer's measured quality stops improving. Our work makes three contributions. First, an honest theoretical footing: we prove deterministic termination and well-definedness and machine-check these claims, while treating the convergence of the distance sequence as an empirically tested conjecture rather than a (previously over-claimed) Banach contraction. Second, a judge-efficient evaluation protocol: we generate each question's full trajectory once, replay every stopping policy over the identical drafts, and cache every LLM-judge call, yielding a strictly paired efficiency-versus-quality comparison at low cost; we further separate operational tokens (charged to a policy) from evaluation tokens (a measurement instrument). Third, an empirical study on multi-hop retrieval-augmented question answering (HotpotQA). On the 60-question test split, a judge-free semantic stopper reduces operational tokens by 38% relative to max_iterations at parity quality (Delta-IS = -0.004, p = 0.81), whereas the full quality-gated variant is counter-productive because its per-round judging dominates cost. An oracle that selects the best round attains +0.115 Information Score over every practical policy (p ~ 4e-11), reframing the problem from "when to stop" (easy) to "which round is best" (open).

items.title: arXiv paper reviews external validity indexes for clustering evaluation with ground truth, recommending centroid index for cluster-level and pair-set index for point-level measures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: How to evaluate clustering with ground truth?
items.summary: A new paper on arXiv reviews common external validity indexes used for evaluating clustering results when ground truth data is available. The authors recommend the centroid index (CI) as an intuitive measure at the cluster level due to its explainable outcomes. For more detailed, point-level evaluation, they suggest the pair-set index (PSI), which offers a normalized score unbiased by cluster sizes, while clustering accuracy (ACC) or other set-matching measures are suitable when all points should be weighted equally.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27061v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: External indexes can be used for cluster evaluation when ground truth is available. We review the most common external validity indexes focusing on set-matching-based measures. We recommend centroid index (CI), because it is an intuitive cluster-level measure with an explainable result. If we need a more fine-tuned, point-level measure, there are more choices. Pair-set index (PSI) provides a normalized score which is not biased by cluster sizes. If all points should matter equally, then clustering accuracy (ACC) or any other set-matching measure is suitable.

items.title: Researchers present JERP, a method for joint learning of experiential rules and policies in large language model agents, improving decision performance in complex interactive tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for Large Language Model Agents
items.summary:
Researchers have developed JERP, a method that jointly learns experiential rules and policies for large language model (LLM) agents operating in multi-step interactive environments. JERP updates a long-term rule pool and the agent's policy using the same interaction data, allowing the agent to retrieve relevant rules during decision-making and refine both rules and policy after each episode. This approach maintains alignment between the evolving policy and the rule pool, improving decision performance in complex tasks.

The method addresses limitations of previous approaches that either stored experience as separate natural-language rules or updated model parameters without effectively correcting local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. Experiments on environments like AlfWorld and WebShop demonstrate that JERP consistently enhances the agent's performance by integrating stable behaviors into the model while adapting to new experiences.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27136v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For LLM agents in multi-step interactive environments, a key challenge is to make effective use of accumulated interaction experience. Existing work has typically separated two uses of such experience: keeping it outside the model as natural-language rules for later prompting, or using trajectories and feedback to update the model parameters. The former is easy to interpret but can fall out of sync with the evolving policy; the latter improves the policy more broadly but provides only limited correction for local mistakes in sparse-reward settings. We present Joint Learning of Experiential Rules and Policies for LLM Agents (JERP), which updates a long-term experiential-rule pool and the policy from the same interaction trajectories. At decision time, JERP retrieves task-relevant rules and conditions the agent on them together with the interaction history. After each episode, it uses the collected trajectories both to optimize the policy and to revise the rule pool by comparing current rollouts with reference successful trajectories. This coupling keeps the rule pool aligned with the evolving policy while allowing stable and effective behaviors to be gradually absorbed into the model itself. Experiments on AlfWorld and WebShop show that JERP yields consistent gains in decision performance for complex interactive tasks.

items.title: Researchers introduce OpenRCA 2.0 with PAVE protocol for step-wise causal supervision in root cause analysis, revealing LLMs recover exact root causes in 20.7% of cases across 11 models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: OpenRCA 2.0: From Outcome Labels to Causal Process Supervision
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced OpenRCA 2.0, a new benchmark for root cause analysis (RCA) that includes step-wise causal annotations using the PAVE protocol. This approach addresses a key limitation in existing datasets by labeling not only the root cause but also the causal propagation path from cause to observed symptom, enabling more rigorous evaluation of large language models (LLMs) in multi-step reasoning and long-context understanding. Testing 11 advanced LLMs on OpenRCA 2.0 revealed that they correctly identify the exact root cause in only 20.7% of cases on average.

The study found that while LLMs often identify at least one correct root cause in 76.0% of cases, they struggle to verify the causal path linking the cause to the symptom, succeeding in only 61.5% of cases. This gap highlights a failure mode that outcome-only evaluations miss, underscoring the importance of step-wise causal supervision for developing trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27154v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Root cause analysis (RCA) poses a holistic test of LLM agentic capabilities, such as long-context understanding, multi-step reasoning, and tool use. However, existing datasets suffer from a fundamental gap: they label only the root cause, not the propagation path connecting it to the observed symptom, which largely simplifies the task to naive pattern matching. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce PAVE, a step-wise labeling protocol that leverages known interventions from fault injection to reconstruct causal propagation paths. The mechanism is forward verification: reasoning from cause to effect rather than inferring backward from symptoms. Applying PAVE yields OpenRCA 2.0 (500 instances), the first cross-system RCA benchmark with step-wise causal annotations for LLM agents. Across 11 frontier LLMs, recovering the exact root-cause set succeeds in only 20.7% of cases on average. To locate where this difficulty lies, we relax the criterion and find what we call the ungrounded diagnosis: agents identify at least one correct root-cause service in 76.0% of cases, but ground that service in a verified causal propagation path to the observed symptom in only 61.5%. Outcome-only evaluation hides this failure mode; step-wise causal ground truth is the missing piece for trustworthy LLM-based RCA agents.

items.title: Researchers propose TOPS, a training-free visual token pruning method for MLLMs that removes up to 77.8% of tokens while preserving or improving performance on LLaVA-NeXT models [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TOPS: First-Principles Visual Token Pruning via Constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets for Efficient MLLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic visual token pruning method designed to improve the efficiency of multimodal large language models (MLLMs) by removing up to 77.8% of visual tokens without sacrificing performance. Applied to LLaVA-NeXT models, TOPS maintained or slightly improved performance on both 7B and 13B parameter versions, demonstrating its ability to reduce computational overhead while preserving model accuracy.

The approach is based on a first-principles formulation called Token Optimal Preservation Sets, guided by three principles: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Extensive testing across seven MLLM architectures and fourteen benchmarks showed that TOPS outperforms existing pruning methods, which often struggle with redundancy or lack alignment with user instructions.

By effectively pruning redundant visual tokens, TOPS not only enhances inference efficiency but also has the potential to reduce hallucinations in MLLMs. This advancement could influence future designs of lightweight multimodal models, making them more practical for real-world applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27161v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved strong multimodal reasoning capabilities, but their efficiency is limited by the large number of visual tokens, which introduces substantial computational overhead. Visual token pruning offers a natural solution, yet existing methods are imperfect: attention-based criteria tend to retain redundant tokens, while diversity-based criteria are often agnostic to user instructions. Even methods that combine multiple criteria still lack a principled formulation of the intrinsic objective of token pruning. In this paper, we revisit visual token pruning from a first-principles perspective and formulate it as constructing Token Optimal Preservation Sets. Through a top-down information-theoretic analysis, we identify three fundamental principles for effective token selection: Task Relevance, Information Coverage, and Semantic Diversity. Based on these principles, we propose TOPS, a training-free and model-agnostic pruning module that can be applied to various MLLMs. Extensive experiments on 7 MLLM backbones and 14 benchmarks demonstrate that TOPS outperforms prior methods under diverse pruning settings. Notably, on LLaVA-NeXT, TOPS removes 77.8% of visual tokens while preserving 100.0% and 100.6% performance on its 7B and 13B models, respectively, suggesting that pruning redundant visual tokens can sometimes mitigate hallucination and inspire future lightweight MLLM design.

items.title: Researchers introduce process harness mechanism to integrate agentic layers with legacy workflows using the Task-Decision-Flow model and CUGA FLO implementation for adaptive business process management [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: A Process Harness for Uplifting Legacy Workflows to Agentic BPM: Design and Realization in CUGA FLO
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the process harness, a novel mechanism that integrates agentic layers with existing legacy workflows in business process management without replacing the underlying workflow engines. This approach uses a policy-governed agentic layer that intercepts key control points to provide reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while maintaining the deterministic workflow engine's structural control. The process harness is formalized through the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, which organizes reasoning across three types of agents—TaskAgent, DecisionAgent, and FlowAgent—each operating under explicit policies within the system's overall governance framework.

The team implemented this model in CUGA FLO and demonstrated its effectiveness using a loan approval workflow that leverages all three agent types and supports regulatory overrides through hook mechanisms. This design uniquely balances imperative requirements, enforced by deterministic workflow execution, with normative requirements, enabled by policy-driven agent autonomy at designated control points, allowing adaptive and compliant business process management.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce the process harness, a new mechanism for uplifting legacy workflows into Agentic Business Process Management (Agentic BPM) without replacing the underlying workflow engine. A process harness places a policy-governed agentic layer around a deterministic workflow engine, intercepting designated control points to contribute reasoning, adaptation, and oversight while the engine retains structural authority over the process. To define the process harness rigorously, we develop the Task-Decision-Flow (TDF) model, specifying both its data schema and its execution semantics. TDF decomposes LLM reasoning across three policy-governed agent types: a TaskAgent for knowledge-intensive task execution, a DecisionAgent for per-case gateway routing, and a FlowAgent that governs runtime flow adaptation through a principled hook mechanism. Each agent reasons within an explicit policy drawn from the process FRAME, the aggregate policy set governing all LLM calls in the system. We then present CUGA FLO as the design and implementation realization of the TDF model, and demonstrate it on a loan approval workflow that exercises all three agent types and hook-driven regulatory override. The process harness uniquely reconciles imperative requirements, realized through deterministic workflow execution that enforces structural compliance, with normative requirements, realized through policy-framed agentic autonomy invoked at designated control points wherever the process demands it.

items.title: Researchers propose GAversary, a genetic algorithm using GloVe embeddings to generate black-box adversarial attacks that reduce natural language model accuracy from 76.8% to 5.8% on benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Vulnerability of Natural Language Classifiers to Evolutionary Generated Adversarial Text
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced GAversary, a genetic algorithm that uses GloVe embeddings to generate black-box adversarial attacks on natural language models. This method requires only the model's output logits to guide its search and significantly reduces model accuracy on benchmark tests, dropping it from 76.8% to as low as 5.8%. GAversary outperforms existing attacks like BAE and A2T in effectiveness, though it modifies more words and slightly decreases semantic similarity to the original text.

GAversary's approach improves upon previous genetic algorithms by leveraging GloVe embeddings for word replacement mutations, enhancing the semantic relevance of adversarial examples. The algorithm was tested on multiple benchmark datasets and well-known models, demonstrating its ability to substantially degrade model performance while operating as a black-box attack. The trade-offs include increased word perturbations and a modest rise in runtime compared to other methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27215v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Deep learning models have achieved impressive performance across various fields but remain vulnerable to adversarial inputs, particularly in NLP, where such attacks can have significant real-world consequences. Adversarial attacks often involve small, semantically similar token replacements to fool NLP models, and recent methods have become more precise by targeting specific vulnerable words, often by exploiting some level of access to the model's internal structure. This paper proposes GAversary, a hybrid Genetic Algorithm (GA) to generate adversarial attacks on natural language models. The GA is able to treat the target model as a black box, requiring only the logit value output by the model to guide the search. GAversary differs from GAs previously proposed for this problem by using GloVe embeddings to propose word replacements (the mutation operator) to improve the semantic similarity of the adversarial examples. GAversary is applied to several benchmark data sets and well-known target models. GAversary is able to substantially reduce the target model's accuracy on test data compared to the BAE and A2T attacks compared against (in the best case, reducing a 76.8% accuracy to 5.8%, compared to BAE's 27.6%). The trade-off is that GAversary perturbs just under twice as many words as the other two methods, with a slightly lower semantic similarity to the original text and around a 5% increase in run-time.

items.title: Researchers propose BINEVAL, a binary-question framework for interpretable LLM evaluation and self-improvement, showing strong results on factual consistency benchmarks and enabling prompt optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Ask, Don't Judge: Binary Questions for Interpretable LLM Evaluation and Self-Improvement
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced BINEVAL, a novel framework designed to improve the evaluation of large language model (LLM) outputs by breaking down assessment criteria into simple binary questions. This approach generates detailed, interpretable feedback and overall scores that are easier to understand and use for prompt refinement. BINEVAL has demonstrated strong performance on benchmarks like SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, particularly excelling in assessing factual consistency compared to existing methods such as UniEval and G-Eval.

The framework operates by using a meta-prompt to create fine-grained evaluation questions, which an LLM answers independently for each output. This method not only aligns well with human judgment distributions but also avoids common issues like ceiling effects, enabling better differentiation between marginal and clearly flawed outputs. Additionally, BINEVAL's question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, enhancing both evaluator and generation prompts across different tasks and models.

Overall, BINEVAL offers a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation system that combines robust empirical results with practical diagnostic and optimization benefits, addressing key challenges in LLM output evaluation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27226v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Evaluating LLM outputs remains a major bottleneck in NLP: human evaluation is expensive and slow, lexical metrics correlate poorly with human judgments on open-ended generation, and holistic LLM judges often produce opaque scores that are hard to debug. We propose BINEVAL, a framework that decomposes evaluation criteria into atomic binary questions and aggregates the resulting verdicts into interpretable, multi-dimensional scores. Given a task prompt, a meta-prompt generates fine-grained evaluation questions, and an LLM answers them independently for each output, yielding transparent question-level feedback together with calibrated overall scores. This decomposition makes evaluation easier to inspect, easier to diagnose, and directly usable for prompt improvement. Across SummEval, Topical-Chat, and QAGS, BINEVAL matches or outperforms strong baselines including UniEval and G-Eval, with especially strong results on factual consistency benchmarks such as QAGS. Beyond competitive correlation with human judgments, BINEVAL better matches human score distributions and avoids the ceiling effects common in prior LLM judges, leading to better discrimination between borderline and clearly flawed outputs. We further show that the same question-level feedback supports iterative prompt optimization, improving evaluator prompts on summarization and generation prompts on IFBench under both self-update and cross-model update settings. Overall, BINEVAL provides a task-agnostic, training-free, and interpretable evaluation framework that combines strong empirical performance with practical diagnostic and optimization value.

items.title: Researchers introduce EO-WM, a physically informed video diffusion transformer for probabilistic Earth observation forecasting that improves vegetation decline prediction under extreme weather conditions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EO-WM: A Physically Informed World Model for Probabilistic Earth Observation Forecasting
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer designed for probabilistic Earth observation forecasting that improves predictions of vegetation decline under extreme weather conditions. This model treats Earth observation forecasting as a weather-driven world modeling problem, incorporating meteorological forcing through a physically informed conditioning framework that separates climatological baselines, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. EO-WM enhances the accuracy of vegetation degradation forecasts by better capturing sustained heat and drought stress compared to existing methods.

To assess the model's performance beyond standard reconstruction metrics, the researchers introduced two diagnostic benchmarks: the Extreme Summer Benchmark, which evaluates severity-aware predictions of vegetation decline during extreme weather, and the Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark, which tests forecast responsiveness to changed weather conditions. Experiments demonstrated that EO-WM reduces error in predicting vegetation decline amplitude by 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by 7.80%, while maintaining competitive performance on pixel-level metrics. The model and benchmarks will be made publicly available to support further research in Earth observation forecasting.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27277v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Earth Observation (EO) forecasting aims to predict future Earth surface dynamics from satellite observations under changing meteorological conditions. In this paper, we view this task as a partially observed, weather-driven world modeling problem, in which weather acts as a conditioning signal, while forecasting remains uncertain due to sparse observations and unobserved land-surface states. However, existing methods do not fully capture this setting: deterministic models collapse uncertainty into a single future prediction, while diffusion-based methods typically treat weather variables as undifferentiated conditioning signals, and existing benchmarks focus mainly on reconstruction accuracy rather than whether forecasts respond correctly to changed weather forcing.We introduce EO-WM, a video diffusion transformer for multispectral EO forecasting. EO-WM incorporates a physically informed conditioning framework that represents meteorological forcing through a climatological baseline, weather anomalies, and cumulative physical stress signals. Specifically, it separates baseline and anomaly through distinct conditioning pathways, and accumulates anomalous forcing over time to capture sustained heat and drought stress. To evaluate weather-response behavior beyond standard metrics, we introduce two diagnostic benchmarks: an Extreme Summer Benchmark for severity-aware prediction of vegetation degradation under extreme weather, and a Seasonal Matched-Pair Benchmark for testing response fidelity under changed weather forcing. Experiments show that EO-WM reduces the error in predicted Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI) decline amplitude by a relative 5.63% and improves directional hit rate by a relative 7.80%, while remaining competitive on standard pixel-level metrics. The benchmarks and model will be made open-source at https://github.com/Luo-Z13/EO-WM.

items.title: Researchers compare simulation-based inference with MCMC for rapid Bayesian calibration of COVID-19 epidemiological models using ICU data from Germany in 2020 [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Simulation-based inference for rapid Bayesian parameter estimation in epidemiological models: a comparison with MCMC
items.summary:
Researchers have evaluated simulation-based inference (SBI) as a faster alternative to Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 ICU occupancy data from Germany in 2020. The study compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases, including both short 31-day inference windows and a longer 201-day reconstruction involving multiple transmission changes. SBI produced posterior distributions closely matching those from MCMC while significantly reducing computational time by leveraging GPU resources.

The analysis showed that SBI accurately reproduced observed ICU trajectories and maintained the dominant posterior structure even in the more complex 201-day scenario, despite increased uncertainty. While MCMC required about 1000 seconds for the 31-day problems and over 19,000 seconds for the 201-day problem, SBI achieved comparable results in approximately 60-70 seconds and 157 seconds respectively. These findings suggest that SBI offers a rapid and computationally efficient framework for near-real-time Bayesian calibration of epidemiological models, facilitating timely outbreak analysis and public health decision-making.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27286v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mechanistic epidemiological models are widely used to support infectious disease forecasting and public-health decision making. Bayesian calibration of such models is commonly performed using Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC), which can become computationally expensive for high-dimensional nonlinear systems and repeated near-real-time analyses. Here, we investigate simulation-based inference (SBI) using neural posterior estimation as a scalable alternative for Bayesian calibration of a mechanistic SECIR epidemiological model using COVID-19 intensive care unit (ICU) occupancy data from Germany during 2020. We compared SBI and MCMC across multiple epidemic phases using both 31-day inference windows and a substantially more challenging 201-day reconstruction problem involving multiple transmission change points. Posterior agreement was evaluated quantitatively using Wasserstein distances and Kullback-Leibler divergences together with posterior predictive checks. Across the 31-day windows, SBI recovered posterior distributions in strong agreement with MCMC while accurately reproducing observed ICU trajectories. In the 201-day setting, SBI preserved the dominant posterior structure despite increased uncertainty. SBI, by combining CPU and GPU resources, substantially reduced computational runtime compared with MCMC, which was restricted to running on CPUs. Whereas MCMC required approximately 1000 seconds for the 31-day inference problems, SBI achieved comparable posterior and predictive performance in approximately 60-70 seconds on a single GPU. For the 201-day inference problem, SBI required an average of 157 seconds, while the MCMC runs took over 19,000 seconds. Our results demonstrate that SBI provides a rapid and computationally efficient framework for Bayesian calibration of mechanistic epidemiological models, supporting repeated near-real-time inference and rapid outbreak analysis.

items.title: Researchers study prompt injection in automated résumé screening with large language models, finding manipulation improves rankings when rare but collapses as it becomes widespread, raising fairness concerns [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Prompt Injection in Automated R\'esum\'e Screening with Large Language Models: Single and Multi-Injection Settings
items.summary:
Researchers have examined the impact of prompt injection—subtle self-promotional text without new qualifications—on automated résumé screening using large language models (LLMs). Their controlled experiments reveal that prompt injection can improve applicant rankings when résumé quality is similar and few candidates use this tactic, but its effectiveness declines sharply as more candidates engage in manipulation, eventually collapsing when widespread. In cases with varied candidate quality, prompt injection is generally less effective but can sometimes allow lower-quality applicants to outrank higher-quality ones, raising concerns about fairness.

The study highlights that LLM-based hiring systems are most vulnerable to manipulation when candidate quality differences are small and prompt injection is rare. The researchers have made their code and resources publicly available to support further investigation into this issue.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27287v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to screen and rank job applicants, creating incentives for candidates to strategically manipulate algorithmic hiring systems. We study prompt injection in automated r\'esum\'e screening, defined as subtle self-promotional text that introduces no new qualifications but is designed to influence LLM evaluations. Using controlled experiments, we show that prompt injection reliably improves applicant rankings when r\'esum\'e quality is homogeneous and few candidates inject. However, its effectiveness rapidly diminishes as more candidates inject, collapsing when manipulation becomes widespread. When candidate quality is heterogeneous, prompt injection is less effective on average, but can occasionally allow lower-quality candidates to outrank higher-quality ones, raising fairness concerns. Overall, LLM-based screening is most vulnerable when manipulation is rare and candidate quality differences are small. Code and resources are publicly available at: https://github.com/preetb1199/Prompt_Injection_ACL26

items.title: Researchers analyze co-failure rates limiting accuracy gains from combining 67 large language models across routing, voting, and mixture-of-agents methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: When Does Combining Language Models Help? A Co-Failure Ceiling on Routing, Voting, and Mixture-of-Agents Across 67 Frontier Models
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed the limitations of combining multiple large language models (LLMs) through methods like routing, voting, and mixture-of-agents to improve accuracy. They identified a key constraint, termed beta, which represents the rate at which all models fail on the same query, capping the maximum achievable accuracy. Their study across 67 models from 21 providers revealed that traditional metrics like average pairwise error correlation do not capture this co-failure rate, which significantly impacts the potential gains from multi-model systems.

The team applied statistical bounds to estimate beta and found that existing models underestimate the frequency of simultaneous failures, especially in tasks like open-ended mathematics and code execution. They also observed that the format of questions influences co-failure rates, with free-response formats showing higher beta values than multiple-choice. Their findings suggest that improvements in multi-model accuracy primarily come from models failing on different queries rather than simply increasing the number of models combined.

These insights highlight the importance of understanding co-failure dynamics when designing ensemble LLM systems and suggest that without strong query-level routing signals, combining models may rarely outperform the best single model on verifiable tasks. This research provides a framework for better evaluating and optimizing multi-model approaches in artificial intelligence.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27288v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-model LLM systems such as routing, voting, cascades, fusion, and mixture-of-agents are used to beat single-model accuracy. We show that their gain is capped by a quantity the field rarely reports. For any policy whose output is one member model answer, accuracy cannot exceed one minus beta, where beta is the rate at which every model is wrong on the same query. In contrast, the usual diagnostic, average pairwise error correlation rho, cannot identify beta: error laws with identical marginals and pairwise correlations can have different all-wrong rates. A Clopper-Pearson bound on beta gives a finite-sample certificate on the largest gain any router, vote, or cascade could deliver before training a router. Across 67 models from 21 providers, a tetrachoric-calibrated single-factor model still underprices the all-wrong tail: on open-ended mathematics, observed beta is 0.052 versus 0.023 under the full 67-model Gaussian copula, about 2.5 times underpricing, with 90 percent CI 1.7 to 3.4 and k equals 17. The effect recurs on execution-graded code, where beta is 0.079. Re-asking the same GPQA-Diamond questions in free-response rather than multiple-choice form reopens the tail, with beta 0.127 and a five-judge panel with kappa 0.73 to 0.92, locating co-failure in answer format rather than subject. At matched quality, low-rho heterogeneous ensembles beat high-rho Self-MoA, but on checkable tasks in our pool, combining models rarely beats the single best model without a strong query-level routing signal. Gains come from models failing on different questions, not from adding more models.

items.title: Researchers benchmark four open-weight language models on Global AI Dataset v2 to assess geographic bias and accuracy in AI governance across 227 countries from 2010 to 2023 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Benchmarking Open-Weight Foundation Models for Global AI Technical Governance
items.summary:
Researchers evaluated four open-weight large language models (LLMs) using the Global AI Dataset v2, which includes 24,453 verified indicators across 227 countries from 2010 to 2023, to assess geographic bias and accuracy in AI governance analysis. The study addressed limitations of previous research by focusing on open models, using data within the models' training periods, and applying a detailed five-category classification of model responses to distinguish between accurate answers, confident fabrications, and honest uncertainty.

The evaluation involved approximately 2,990 country-metric-year observations across six years, covering 18 indicators aligned with the IEEE IRAI 2026 framework. Researchers used mixed-effects logistic regression and difference-in-differences analysis to measure disparities in model accuracy related to geographic representation in training data, highlighting the challenges LLMs face when analyzing underrepresented countries in AI governance contexts.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26099v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed in artificial intelligence (AI) governance analysis across national and international organisations. There is, however, growing evidence that such models produce significantly less accurate responses for countries that are underrepresented in their training data-a pattern described in existing literature as geographic bias. Existing studies examining this phenomenon are subject to three methodological limitations that together undermine their findings: (1) reliance on proprietary systems whose weights are not publicly released, which prevents independent replication; (2) evaluation of model knowledge about years that fall after data collection for model training had concluded, leading to geographic ignorance in addition to the natural limits of each model's knowledge; and (3) use of coarse binary response classification that cannot distinguish models' confident fabrication (HF) from their honest acknowledgement of uncertainty. This study addresses all three limitations by benchmarking four open-weight frontier language models against the Global AI Dataset v2 (GAID v2), a verified ground-truth database of 24,453 indicators across 227 countries published on Harvard Dataverse in January 2026. A total of 18 indicators, mapped to the eight thematic dimensions of the IEEE IRAI 2026 framework, are selected from GAID v2, yielding approximately 2,990 country-metric-year observations across six evaluation years (within the period of 2010-2023). Model responses are classified using a five-category scheme that distinguishes (a) verified accuracy (VA), (b) HF, (c) honest refusal (HR), (d) qualitative hedging (QH), and (e) misattribution (MF). Geographic disparities in accuracy are estimated through mixed-effects logistic regression and difference-in-differences (DiD) analysis.

items.title: Researchers present Know2Guess, a contamination-aware multi-zone benchmark with 1,200 items for evaluating knowledge boundaries and abstention behavior in large language models [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Know2Guess: A Contamination-Aware Multi-Zone Benchmark for Knowledge-Boundary Evaluation in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Know2Guess, a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark designed to evaluate large language models' ability to distinguish between supported answers and unsupported guesses while accounting for data contamination and refusal behaviors. The benchmark includes 1,200 items across five domains with explicit abstention expectations and contamination-risk metadata, enabling assessment of models' transitions from answering to abstaining under controlled conditions.

The study tested models such as FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct using various prompt strategies and parsing methods. Results showed that while instruction-tuned models demonstrated some ability to selectively abstain, challenges remain in calibration and handling answer-expected zones. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieved the highest reliability, but no model fully solved the benchmark, highlighting ongoing difficulties in balancing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination. The dataset and evaluation protocol are publicly available for further research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26101v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Reliable evaluation of large language models should separate supported answering from unsupported guessing without conflating either with data contamination, prompt idiosyncrasy, or generic refusal behavior. We present a contamination-aware, multi-zone benchmark for measuring the transition from answerable knowledge to abstention-expected unknowns under frozen build-time labels. The benchmark contains 1,200 items across five domains, explicit abstention expectations, contamination-risk metadata, and dual parsing with an official strict parser plus a normalized robustness parser. We evaluate FLAN-T5, Qwen2.5-Instruct, and Llama-3-Instruct models under locked answer-or-abstain prompts, answer-only controls, and prompt-template variants. The benchmark is not solved by generic non-answer behavior: FLAN baselines remain weak on productive abstention, while stronger instruction-tuned models expose a selective but incomplete transition from answering to abstaining. Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct achieves the best overall reliability, but answer-expected zones remain difficult, calibration remains poor, and benign-item refusal persists. Prompt and parser robustness analyses preserve the main ranking and qualitative conclusions. The benchmark therefore provides a reproducible protocol for auditing answerability, abstention, refusal, and contamination as distinct but interacting dimensions of LLM reliability.The dataset is publicly available at https://github.com/renweimeng/Know2Guess-A-Contamination-Aware-Multi-Zone-Benchmark.

items.title: Researchers find post-training on helpfulness data degrades mid-trained compassion values in Llama 3.1 8B model, with coding-domain post-training better preserving values and reasoning [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Helpfulness Hurts: Domain-Dependent Degradation of Mid-Trained Compassion Values Under Post-Training
items.summary:
Researchers examined how different post-training domains affect the retention of compassion values in the Llama 3.1 8B language model, which was mid-trained on compassion-oriented data. They found that post-training focused on helpfulness significantly reduced the model's animal compassion and moral reasoning abilities compared to coding-domain post-training, as measured by the Animal Harm Benchmark and the Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty benchmark. This degradation was consistent across two training methods and datasets but did not appear in multilingual moral reasoning tests.

The study revealed that compassion values instilled during mid-training are more deeply encoded and transfer better across languages than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. Coding-domain post-training preserved these mid-trained values more effectively than helpfulness-focused training, without impairing general reasoning skills. These findings suggest that for models trained with value-laden data, selecting the post-training domain carefully is crucial to maintaining desired ethical attributes.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26102v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Standard post-training pipelines apply supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL) to make language models helpful, but these processes may inadvertently degrade values instilled during pre-training. We investigate whether the domain of post-training data differentially affects the retention of animal compassion values in a Llama 3.1 8B model mid-trained on compassion-oriented synthetic data, using both SFT (helpfulness via Dolly-15k vs. coding via Magicoder-110K) and GRPO (helpfulness via RLHFlow vs. coding via Magicoder), evaluated on the Animal Harm Benchmark (AHB 2.2) and MORU benchmark (Moral Reasoning Under Uncertainty). Helpfulness training significantly degrades animal compassion relative to coding training on AHB (SFT: 35.7% vs. 65.2%; GRPO: 18.7% vs. 32.0%), replicating across two independent helpfulness datasets and two training paradigms. On English MORU items, helpfulness training degrades general moral reasoning by 25.5 percentage points (46.4% vs. 71.9%), a striking gap that rivals the compassion effect in magnitude. However, this effect does not transfer cross-lingually: on the multilingual MORU benchmark, the domain effect disappears (SFT: 52.3% vs. 51.2%). In contrast, the animal compassion effect transfers consistently across languages, with Magicoder's AHB percentage-point gain over the base model 4.5 times larger on non-English items than English items. This divergence suggests that values instilled through mid-training are encoded more deeply and cross-lingually than reasoning improvements from domain-specific post-training. These results suggest that, for labs building on value-laden mid-training, coding-domain post-training may better preserve mid-trained values than helpfulness post-training without harming general reasoning capabilities.

items.title: Study finds large language models perform well on text-only statics problems but accuracy drops with diagrams and multi-step reasoning challenges [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Investigating LLM's Problem Solving Capability -- a Study on Statics Questions
items.summary:
A recent study evaluated the problem-solving abilities of large language models (LLMs), specifically ChatGPT, on statics questions commonly found in mechanical engineering education. The research found that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy declines when diagrams are included and when problems require multi-step reasoning. This suggests that the models struggle more with complex reasoning and consistently applying visual information than with image recognition itself.

The study used a model distillation approach to extract 25 text-only statics questions and created additional datasets by adding diagrams and altering numerical values. The findings highlight the limitations of current LLMs in handling engineering problems that combine visual and textual information, emphasizing the need for improved multi-step reasoning capabilities in these models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26103v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have rapidly influenced many aspects of society, particularly education, due to their demonstrated ability to complete assignments and examinations across a wide range of subjects. Although prior studies have examined the educational impact of LLMs, much of the existing work relies on public or open problem datasets and lacks topic-specific analysis. In engineering education, especially within mechanical engineering, systematic investigations of LLM performance on specific problem types remain limited. Instead of using traditional methods that directly ask textbook questions to an LLM tool, our study adopts a model distillation process to evaluate LLM capabilities in solving statics problems. By distilling ChatGPT, we extracted 25 text-only statics questions and further constructed two additional datasets by adding diagrams and modifying their numerical values. Experimental results show that while LLMs perform well on text-only statics problems, their accuracy decreases when diagrams are introduced and the problems require multi-step reasoning. Further analysis suggests that this performance drop is not primarily caused by limitations in image recognition, but rather by difficulties in multi-step reasoning and in consistently applying extracted visual information across successive solution stages.

items.title: Researchers find assertive and explicit linguistic features in fine-tuning data increase Llama-3.2-1B's pro-animal-welfare reasoning, while hedged and sensory descriptions dilute it [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Assert, don't describe: Linguistic features that shift LLM reasoning about animal welfare
items.summary:
Researchers analyzed how different linguistic features in fine-tuning data influence Llama-3.2-1B's reasoning about animal welfare. They found that assertive and explicit language, including moral vocabulary, emotion words, and narrative elements, significantly enhance the model's pro-animal-welfare stance, while hedged language and concrete sensory descriptions tend to weaken it. The study suggests that clearly asserting a position in animal-welfare texts is more effective for training language models than neutral scene descriptions.

items.title: Researchers introduce ContextForge for efficient context recycling in long-horizon LLM inference, improving consistency and reducing token use in 15-turn healthcare query benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Context Recycling for Long-Horizon LLM Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ContextForge, a system designed to improve the performance of large language models (LLMs) in long-horizon conversational tasks by efficiently recycling context. ContextForge combines structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis to maintain relevant information across multiple turns without replaying the entire context, reducing token usage while preserving answer quality. The system was tested on a 15-turn healthcare query benchmark, demonstrating improved consistency and reduced token consumption compared to baseline models, with comparable accuracy.

This approach addresses the limitations of LLMs in handling extended conversations due to context window constraints and inefficient token use. By enabling the reuse of prior computations, ContextForge offers a practical solution for extending LLM capabilities in complex, multi-turn reasoning tasks without the need for larger context windows or retraining. The researchers have made their code and evaluation materials publicly available for further exploration.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26105v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong capabilities in short-context reasoning but degrade in performance over long conversational horizons due to context window limitations and inefficient token usage. We introduce ContextForge, a system for context recycling that maintains task-relevant information across turns by combining structured query generation, external memory retrieval, and controlled synthesis. The system enables efficient reuse of prior computation without relying on full context replay, reducing token overhead while preserving answer quality. We evaluate ContextForge using a 15-turn conversational benchmark that tests multi-turn reasoning, back-references, and domain shifts across structured healthcare queries. Compared to a baseline agent using identical underlying models, ContextForge demonstrates improved consistency and reduced token consumption, while maintaining comparable response accuracy. These results suggest that context recycling provides a practical approach for extending LLM capabilities in long-horizon tasks without requiring larger context windows or model retraining. Code and evaluation artifacts are available at https://github.com/Betanu701/ContextForge.

items.title: Researchers use Nonviolent Communication constraints to reduce conversational escalation in large language model dialogues, improving interaction stability with resistant users [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Reducing Conversational Escalation in Large Language Model Dialogue with Nonviolent Communication Constraints
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a method to reduce conversational escalation in large language model (LLM) dialogues by applying constraints based on Nonviolent Communication (NVC) principles. These constraints guide LLMs to avoid blame, focus on users' emotional experiences, and seek clarification before offering advice, aiming to de-escalate conflicts in emotionally charged interactions.

Using a dual-agent simulation framework across various instruction-tuned models and levels of user resistance, the study demonstrates that NVC-constrained prompting consistently lowers escalation and stabilizes conversations with resistant users. This approach suggests that simple, process-oriented communication guidelines can enhance the trustworthiness and safety of LLM interactions in conflict-prone settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26106v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used in emotionally charged situations involving interpersonal conflict, frustration, and distress. While prior safety research has focused on preventing explicit harms such as toxic or policy-violating content, less attention has been paid to conversational behaviors that may unintentionally escalate conflict. In this paper, we investigate whether LLMs can be guided toward more de-escalating dialogue behavior through lightweight prompt-level constraints derived from Nonviolent Communication (NVC). We reformulate NVC principles as process-oriented guidelines that discourage blame attribution, emphasize attention to users' emotional experiences, and encourage clarification before advice. Using a dual-agent simulation framework across multiple instruction-tuned models and user resistance levels, we show that NVC-constrained prompting consistently reduces conversational escalation and stabilizes interactions with highly resistant users. These results suggest that simple communication constraints can meaningfully improve the trustworthiness of LLM dialogue in conflict-prone settings.

items.title: Researchers present NEST-V1, a lightweight multimodal system translating Nepali spoken words into emotion-conditioned sign language avatars with 81.1% ASR and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Low Resource Multimodal Translation of Nepali Spoken Words into Emotion-Conditioned Sign Language Avatars
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NEST-V1, a lightweight multimodal system that translates Nepali spoken words into emotion-conditioned sign language avatars. The system uses a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous automatic speech recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% accuracy in speech recognition and 79.21% in emotion recognition on a dataset of 600 audio samples. This pilot study focuses on four common Nepali words expressed in three emotional states to validate the approach.

NEST-V1 demonstrates 37% greater parameter efficiency compared to separate models while maintaining a compact size suitable for edge deployment. The framework establishes a foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource languages and offers scalability for expanding vocabulary and emotional expressions. These preliminary results suggest the potential for real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems to benefit the hearing-impaired community, with opportunities for further development.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26107v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sign language communication systems, that integrate emotional expression remain underexplored, particularly for low-resource languages. This pilot study presents NEST-V1 (Nepali Emotion and Speech Transformer - Version 1), a proof-of-concept multimodal framework that demonstrates the feasibility of generating emotion-conditioned Nepali Sign Language avatars from spoken input. As a preliminary investigation, we focus on four common Nepali words ("thank you", "hello", "house", "me") across three emotional states (happy, neutral, sad) to validate our core technical approach. Our lightweight architecture employs a shared acoustic encoder for simultaneous Automatic Speech Recognition and emotion classification, achieving 81.1% ASR accuracy and 79.21% emotion recognition accuracy on a dataset of 600 labeled audio samples from 50 speakers. The system demonstrates 37% parameter efficiency compared to separate model architectures while maintaining a lightweight footprint with only 22.1M parameters suitable for edge deployment. This pilot work establishes the technical foundation for emotion-aware sign language translation in low-resource settings and provides a scalable framework for future expansion to larger vocabularies and more diverse emotional expressions. Our preliminary results indicate the viability of real-time, emotionally expressive sign language communication systems for the hearing-impaired community, with clear pathways for enhancement in subsequent development phases.

items.title: Paper analyzes legal and technical aspects of generative AI music systems under US copyright law, highlighting risks of lyric copying and gaps in vocal likeness protection [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Generative AI and Copyright Infringement: A Legal-Technical Analysis of AI Music Generation Systems Under 17 U.S.C. Title 17
items.summary:
A recent paper analyzes the legal and technical challenges of generative AI music systems under U.S. copyright law, focusing on issues such as unauthorized lyric copying and the use of AI-generated vocals that imitate real artists. It examines whether creating and monetizing songs using protected lyrics combined with synthetic voices violates exclusive rights under Title 17 of the U.S. Code, highlighting the distinction between protections for musical compositions and sound recordings.

The study reviews relevant copyright doctrines, state-level voice-cloning laws, and recent legal cases to map AI technical components to associated legal risks. It finds that while unauthorized lyric use poses a significant infringement risk, AI-generated vocal likenesses typically fall outside federal sound recording protections and instead raise state publicity rights concerns. The paper identifies a regulatory gap in federal law regarding synthesized vocal likeness and offers policy recommendations for clearer rules governing AI music creation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26111v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has enabled users to synthesize music with text prompts, combining copyrighted lyrics, AI-composed melodies, and synthetic vocals that imitate real artists. This paper examines the legal and technical dimensions of AI-based music creation (e.g., Google Gemini's music tools) under U.S. copyright law. We analyze whether a user who inputs one artist's protected lyrics into a GenAI system, directs it to use another artist's voice or style, publishes the resulting song, and monetizes it violates 17 U.S.C. Section 106's exclusive rights [3]. The analysis integrates Title 17 doctrine (rights of reproduction, derivative works, distribution), 17 U.S.C. Section 114's narrow sound recording protection [4], and the new voice-cloning laws emerging at the state level [20]. We argue that unauthorized lyric copying poses a high risk of infringement of the musical composition, whereas mere AI-generated voice imitation typically falls outside federal sound recording protection and instead implicates state publicity rights [12], [13]. Recent cases and legislation (Concord v. Anthropic [10]; Kadrey v. Meta [11]; Lehrman v. Lovo [12]; Tennessee's "ELVIS Act" [20]; UMG v. Uncharted Labs [14]; etc.) illustrate this split. We map AI technical components (prompt encoding, latent diffusion, neural vocoders, speaker embeddings) to legal risks and identify a regulatory gap: federal law robustly protects lyrics and melody but currently provides limited remedies for synthesized vocal likeness [22], [23]. The paper concludes with policy suggestions for clearer rules on AI music creation.

items.title: Researchers present a structured-data pipeline converting Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million instruction-response pairs to fine-tune a 12B-parameter model for specialized conversational AI in low-resource languages [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Lexicon to AI: A Structured-Data Pipeline for Specialized Conversational Systems in Low-Resource Languages
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a structured-data pipeline that transforms Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million instruction-response pairs to fine-tune a 12-billion-parameter language model. This approach uses resource-efficient techniques like LoRA with 4-bit quantization to create a specialized conversational AI system tailored for low-resource languages. Evaluations with a Hindi language learning chatbot show that this system outperforms general-purpose models in pedagogical effectiveness while maintaining strong semantic performance and consistency.

The methodology demonstrates how expert-curated lexical databases can serve as a foundation for developing specialized AI without relying on large training corpora. This proof-of-concept using Hindi suggests the approach can be applied to any language with existing WordNet resources, addressing a significant gap in AI accessibility for many low-resource languages and offering a practical alternative to data-intensive methods.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26112v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Low-resource languages face a critical challenge in AI development: creating specialized conversational systems without access to massive training corpora. We present a systematic methodology for transforming structured linguistic resources into specialized AI systems, demonstrating that expert-curated lexical databases can serve as effective foundations for conversational AI development. Our approach converts Hindi WordNet into 1.25 million diverse instruction-response pairs, fine-tunes a 12B-parameter language model using resource-efficient LoRA with 4-bit quantization. Evaluation through a Hindi language learning chatbot demonstrates that structured-knowledge-based systems achieve superior pedagogical effectiveness (91.0 vs. 79.4-83.6 for general-purpose models) while maintaining competitive semantic performance and exceptional consistency. The complete pipeline demonstrates a proof-of-concept methodology using Hindi for developing specialized AI systems for any languages with WordNet resources. This work addresses the critical gap in AI accessibility for low-resource languages, offering a practical alternative to corpus-intensive approaches and potentially enabling specialized AI development for the hundreds of languages with existing WordNet resources.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26114v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We examine the structural transformation of creative industries under generative artificial intelligence, drawing on 374 primary sources spanning policy documents, industry data, creator surveys, and platform analytics. Beginning with the December 2024 release of OpenAI's Sora video model as a watershed event, we trace the historical pattern of creative resistance to technological disruption, then develop an analytical framework -- the Human-AI Agency Continuum for mapping the spectrum of human and machine collaboration in creative work. We present evidence for the "slop ceiling," an audience-imposed quality threshold that constrains AI-generated content to approximately 1--3% of platform streams despite comprising 44% of uploads. Analysis of the UK Government's 2025 consultation on AI and copyright (over 11,500 responses, 88% opposing expanded AI training rights) reveals deep structural tensions between technology firms and creative workers. We investigate how major studios, from Disney's $1 billion OpenAI investment to Netflix's AI-native animation unit, are positioning for an AI-augmented production pipeline. The work covers coordination collapse in creative supply chains, the emergence of new professional roles such as prompt engineers and AI orchestrators, and proposes four principles for navigating the transition: transparency, consent, compensation, and human-centred design. Eight appendices provide quantitative analysis, a glossary, topical bibliography, and deep dives into shadow AI adoption, AI stigma, and algorithmic intent.

items.originalTitle: A Multi-Layer AI Framework for Information Landscape Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-layer AI framework designed to analyze information landscapes in the context of information disorder. Unlike traditional binary fact-checking approaches, this framework evaluates political and media content across various dimensions such as source reliability, factual structure, framing, bias, emotional activation, manipulation patterns, and propagation dynamics. The aim is to create a structured representation of the informational environment surrounding events, entities, or narratives to support more nuanced media analysis.

The framework emphasizes epistemic mapping, providing a transparent, multi-dimensional view of how facts, interpretations, actors, and narratives interact over time. The paper outlines the conceptual architecture, analytical layers, and methodological rationale behind this approach, aiming to enhance the development of explainable and critically useful AI tools for researching information disorder.

items.title: Study finds ChatGPT and Claude disagree on two-thirds of brand recommendations but converge on diagnosing failure modes 95% of the time across 7,763 joint failures [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Divergent Recommendations, Convergent Diagnoses: Cross-Provider Failure-Mode Convergence in AI Commercial Recommendation
items.summary:
A study analyzing product recommendations from ChatGPT and Claude reveals that the two AI providers disagree on brand recommendations about two-thirds of the time. However, when both fail to recommend a brand, they concur on the failure mode—discoverability, compellingness, or positioning—95% of the time across 7,763 joint failures. This high agreement increases as brand prominence decreases, reaching nearly complete consensus for less well-known regional brands.

The research highlights that ChatGPT and Claude use different generative approaches to select brands, with Anthropic relying more on prior knowledge than OpenAI. Despite these differences, their convergence on diagnosing failure modes is particularly significant for improving recommendations for long-tail brands. Addressing these failure modes enhances brand visibility on both platforms, though strategies for category leaders require more provider-specific adjustments.
