items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26116v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: A brand whose customers use both ChatGPT and Claude for product recommendations faces a strategic choice: a single optimization playbook, or one per provider? Across 215 commercially-framed prompts in four measurement batches, the two providers disagree on which brands they recommend roughly two-thirds of the time (cross-provider recommendation Jaccard 0.35, below the 0.50-0.61 same-prompt rerun baseline). The picks diverge. But when neither provider recommends a brand, we classify the failure into one of three modes -- discoverability (the brand never reaches the model), compellingness (it reaches the model but isn't mentioned), or positioning (it's mentioned but not recommended) -- and on 7,763 such joint failures, both providers diagnose the same failure mode 95.1% of the time (clustered 95% CI [94.3%, 95.7%]). Agreement rises monotonically with falling brand prominence, from 81% [78.2%, 84.0%] on category leaders to 99.6% [99.3%, 99.9%] on long-tail regional brands. The two providers reach their picks by measurably different generative routes -- Anthropic recommends from priors 43-52% of the time, OpenAI 8-29% -- but they converge on the failure diagnosis where it matters most for the long tail. Work that addresses the diagnosed failure mode lifts visibility on both providers; positioning - and content-level work for category leaders is more provider-specific.

items.title: Researchers introduce Governance Inversion Hypothesis explaining how increased AI regulation may reduce organisational operational control through authority fragmentation and procedural complexity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Governance Inversion Hypothesis: Why More AI Regulation May Produce Less Organisational Control
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed the Governance Inversion Hypothesis (GIH) to address a paradox in AI governance: as regulatory measures and technological complexity increase, organizations may become more formally governed yet lose operational control over AI systems. Contrary to the common belief that stronger regulation enhances accountability and oversight, the study argues that increased governance formalization can fragment authority and complicate procedures, ultimately weakening an organization's ability to manage AI effectively.

The paper outlines four mechanisms—authority fragmentation, symbolic governance expansion, externalization of control, and authority paralysis—that contribute to this decline in operational control. It suggests that layered and complex governance structures can reduce technical visibility and intervention capacity over AI infrastructures. By extending institutional decoupling theory, the authors highlight that expanding governance may paradoxically undermine operational coherence rather than strengthen it.

This research implies that the main risk in AI governance is not the lack of regulatory frameworks but the emergence of institutions that appear well-governed while progressively losing their capacity to govern effectively. This insight calls for a reevaluation of how AI regulations are designed and implemented to ensure they support, rather than hinder, organizational control.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26117v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper introduces the Governance Inversion Hypothesis (GIH) to explain a growing paradox in artificial intelligence (AI) governance: under conditions of increasing regulatory expansion and technological complexity, organisations may become more formally governed while simultaneously experiencing a decline in operational control over AI systems. Existing AI governance frameworks generally assume that stronger regulation improves accountability, oversight, and organisational control. This paper challenges that assumption by arguing that governance formalisation itself may contribute to the erosion of control in AI-intensive environments. Drawing on institutional theory, organisational governance research, accountability scholarship, and emerging AI governance literature, the paper develops a conceptual framework explaining how regulatory expansion may weaken operational authority through four interconnected mechanisms: authority fragmentation, symbolic governance expansion, externalisation of control, and authority paralysis. As governance systems become increasingly layered and procedurally dense, organisations may struggle to maintain coherent authority, technical visibility, escalation capability, and meaningful intervention power over opaque and externally mediated AI infrastructures. The paper extends institutional decoupling theory by introducing governance inversion as a structural condition in which governance expansion may actively undermine operational coherence rather than strengthen it. It concludes that the central risk in AI governance may not be the absence of governance structures, but the emergence of institutions that appear increasingly governed while progressively losing the capacity to govern effectively.

items.title: Researchers develop open-source economic index measuring AI adoption and capability across occupations using user-LLM chat data and O*NET tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Open Source Economic Index of AI Adoption and Capability
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an open-source economic index to measure AI adoption and capability across various occupations by analyzing publicly available user-LLM chat data and O*NET task information. Their findings indicate that sectors such as finance, computer science, and the arts exhibit the highest rates of AI adoption. To assess AI capabilities, the team created benchmark scenarios based on O*NET occupations and tasks, testing the Kimi-k2.5 model with an OpenAI agents SDK across nine frequently represented occupations in their index.

The evaluation revealed that while AI systems can successfully execute high-level workflows, they often struggle with detailed aspects, such as specific tool usage. This work provides a replicable framework for tracking AI integration in the workforce and assessing its practical performance on discrete labor tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26118v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We work towards measuring both AI adoption and the capability of AI to perform discrete labor tasks across various occupations. To measure adoption, we develop an open-source economic index that uses publicly available user-LLM chat data and O*NET tasks to replicate studies produced by frontier AI labs, finding that occupations in the finance, computer science, and arts sectors are those with the highest adoption rates. To measure capabilities, we build a system that generates benchmark scenarios grounded in O*NET occupations, tasks, and model-context-protocol (MCP) servers. We test Kimi-k2.5 with an OpenAI agents SDK harness on scenarios across 9 occupations that appear frequently in our index, finding that AI correctly executes high-level workflows but often errs in the granular details (such as specific tool calls used).

items.title: Researchers present Dot-Flik, a scalable edge AI architecture for distributed insect monitoring with motion-informed frame filtering and hierarchical IoT design, validated on low-cost hardware with real-time performance and energy savings [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Dot-Flik: A Scalable Edge AI Architecture for Distributed Insect Monitoring
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Dot-Flik, a scalable edge AI system designed for distributed insect monitoring that addresses the challenges of high hardware costs, energy consumption, and dependence on centralized processing. The system features a motion-informed frame filtering algorithm that reduces irrelevant data at the edge without requiring deep learning on the sensing device, and a hierarchical IoT architecture that separates data acquisition from AI classification to enhance scalability and coverage.

The approach was validated through outdoor deployments using low-cost hardware, demonstrating significant frame reduction, real-time 30 FPS performance with computational headroom, energy savings up to 22.6%, and support for multiple concurrent edge streams per central node. These results suggest Dot-Flik offers a practical, efficient foundation for dense, low-cost biodiversity monitoring networks, particularly suited for urban environments.

items.summary:

items.title: Researchers propose Geo-FairFed, a geometric fairness-aware routing system using hyperbolic graph neural networks and federated optimization to improve latency, energy use, and fairness in 6G and IoT edge networks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Geometric Fairness-Aware Routing for Federated Edge Networks
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Geo-FairFed, a routing system designed for emerging 6G and edge-intelligent networks that integrates hyperbolic graph neural networks with federated optimization to enhance latency, energy efficiency, and fairness across distributed edge nodes. The system models network topologies on a negatively curved manifold to capture hierarchical and asymmetric connections, while a global aggregator enforces fairness by minimizing routing loss and inequality based on Jain's fairness index. This approach aims to balance performance equitably among nodes rather than focusing solely on aggregate metrics.

Theoretical analysis confirms convergence under certain curvature conditions and demonstrates that the fairness component leads to a Pareto-improving equilibrium in routing performance. Simulations on dynamic 6G-edge and IoT network topologies show that Geo-FairFed reduces average latency by 20%, cuts energy consumption by 17%, and improves fairness by up to 21% compared to existing federated and geometric routing protocols. These results suggest that embedding network topology in hyperbolic space and incorporating fairness into federated learning can significantly improve the efficiency and equity of large-scale network routing.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26125v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Emerging 6G and edge-intelligent networks require effective and balanced routing algorithms among varied and spatially distributed devices. Existing federated routing systems often prioritize aggregate latency or throughput above fairness and the underlying geometric structure of network topologies. This paper describes Geo-FairFed, a geometric fairness-aware routing system that blends hyperbolic graph neural networks (HGNNs) and federated optimization to provide equal performance across edge nodes. Each node learns topology-aware representations on a negatively curved manifold, which include hierarchical relationships and connection asymmetries. A global aggregator next enforces fairness using a curvature-regularized aim that minimizes routing loss, geometric inconsistency, and an inequality penalty based on Jain's fairness index. A theoretical analysis develops convergence guarantees under limited curvature and shows that the proposed fairness term results in a Pareto-improving equilibrium in routing performance. Extensive simulations on dynamic 6G-edge and IoT topologies reveal that Geo-FairFed minimizes average latency by 20\%, reduces energy consumption by 17\%, and improves fairness by up to 21\% when compared to state-of-the-art federated and geometric routing protocols. The study found that embedding topology in a hyperbolic manifold and including fairness into federated updates can significantly enhance the efficiency and equity of large-scale network routing.

items.title: Study finds GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 suggest narrower research methods than recent arXiv computer science papers, with significant provider bias and reduced methodological diversity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Thinking Like a Scientist? A Structural Study of LLM-Generated Research Methods
items.summary:
A recent study analyzed how Large Language Models (LLMs) like GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 suggest research methodologies when prompted with questions extracted from 1,000 recent computer science papers on arXiv. The study found that these LLMs tend to recommend a much narrower range of methods compared to the diverse approaches documented in the papers, with a significant bias toward certain model providers. This narrowing effect was consistent across models and was most pronounced in the choice of model providers, indicating a concentration in default methodological suggestions.

The researchers mapped methods from both LLM outputs and paper inventories into a shared taxonomy and measured divergences across dimensions such as dataset task type and evaluation metrics. They observed that single-occurrence academic models were underrepresented in LLM suggestions, while reused academic or community models were slightly overrepresented. The study also confirmed that LLM outputs are query-specific but filtered through a limited set of options, which may lead researchers relying solely on these suggestions to inadvertently restrict their methodological search space.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26130v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to guide research methodology, yet their default methodological tendencies under minimal prompting remain unclear. Here, we prompt GPT-5.1, Gemini 3 Pro, and DeepSeek-V3.2 with an LLM-extracted research question from each of 1,000 recent arXiv computer-science papers and compare the resulting methodology suggestions against a paper-derived experimental inventory. Since we provide only the research question, the differences we measure reflect initial suggestions and not how optimal those suggestions are. We extract structured method features from both sources, map them into a shared taxonomy, and quantify divergence across multiple taxonomy dimensions including model provider, dataset task type, and evaluation metric type. The strongest imbalance appears in provider choice, with Jensen-Shannon divergence about 3-5x larger than any other taxonomy dimension. Other/Academic single-occurrence models are underrepresented by 23-24 percentage points, while reused academic/community models are slightly overrepresented (4-6pp). LLMs also suggest a much narrower range of methods overall: the effective number of model entities contracts from 1,232 to 59-96, and inter-LLM rank correlations (0.55-0.68) generally exceed LLM-to-paper correlations (0.33-0.56), so the distortions are largely shared across models. Popularity baselines, BM25 retrieval calibration, and paper-level similarity tests confirm that the outputs are query-specific responses, but filtered through a narrower set of options. Researchers who rely on LLM suggestions without cross-checking therefore risk narrowing their methodological search space toward a more concentrated default.

items.title: arXiv:2606.26139 presents a multiscale model coupling strategic exit-join decisions with tactical consensus dynamics to analyze coalition formation and stability in multi-agent systems
items.originalTitle: Multiscale Exit-Join Dynamics: Tactical Consensus and Strategic Coalition Formation
items.summary:
The paper presents a multiscale model that integrates strategic exit-and-join decisions with tactical consensus dynamics to study coalition formation and stability in multi-agent systems. It models coalition value as emerging from within-group information aggregation and uses Aumann-Dreze payoffs, switching frictions, and acceptance rules to govern coalition reconfiguration. The framework features a fast-slow dynamic where coalition value arises from consensus processes, while coalition structures evolve through incentive-driven membership changes.

The analysis identifies conditions for various equilibrium states, including unanimity, segregation, and polarization, and establishes fixed-point characterizations for the coupled dynamics. Numerical experiments reveal an instability-consensus paradox, where low switching barriers can hinder strategic convergence but promote sufficient mixing to achieve global tactical consensus. This work offers a unified approach to understanding coalition formation, consensus mechanisms, information aggregation, and strategic stability in multi-agent environments.

Coalition value is generated endogenously from within-coalition information aggregation, while Aumann-Dreze payoffs, switching frictions, and acceptance rules govern strategic reconfiguration. The framework introduces a fast-slow architecture in which transferable coalition value emerges from DeGroot-style consensus processes, while coalition structures evolve through incentive-driven exit-and-join dynamics. The analysis characterizes joint tactical-strategic equilibria, conditions for tactical and strategic unanimity, segregation, polarization, and cognitive barriers that sustain stable coalition structures. A fixed-point characterization and existence results are established for the coupled dynamics. Numerical experiments reveal an instability-consensus paradox: low or negative switching barriers may prevent strategic convergence while simultaneously promoting temporal mixing sufficient to achieve global tactical consensus. The results provide a unified perspective on coalition formation, consensus dynamics, information aggregation, and strategic stability in multi-agent systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce unsupervised Video Memory Transformers for real-time obstacle detection on autonomous agricultural rover, achieving state-of-the-art results on rapeseed dataset [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Unsupervised Memory-Enhanced Video Transformers: Obstacle Detection for Autonomous Agricultural Rover
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Video Memory Transformers for Anomaly Detection (VMTAD), an unsupervised method designed to detect obstacles in real-time for autonomous agricultural rovers. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional sensors like LiDAR, which cannot detect obstacles beneath plant canopies, and supervised camera-based methods that struggle with unseen obstacles. VMTAD uses a transformer architecture with a memory module that processes temporal context from previous frames, enabling effective detection in dynamic environments without requiring labeled data.

The system was tested on the 'Grillion' agricultural rover using a challenging rapeseed dataset, achieving state-of-the-art results with detection and segmentation AUC scores of 0.973 and 0.997, respectively. A lightweight version of the model balances high accuracy with real-time inference speeds of 14 milliseconds, which is crucial for ensuring operational safety by allowing timely stopping responses.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26151v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While autonomous rovers have become indispensable to precision farming, achieving consistent operational safety remains a critical challenge. Conventional safety sensors, such as LiDAR, fail to detect obstacles positioned below the plant canopy, posing a significant risk. While camera-based supervised learning methods can detect common objects, they perform poorly when faced with obstacles that were not present in their training data. Actual unsupervised anomaly detection offers a solution by learning the normal visual patterns of an environment, but often fails for the dynamic scenes captured by a moving rover.\\ This paper introduces Video Memory Transformers for Anomaly Detection (VMTAD), a fully unsupervised method designed for real-time obstacle detection in dynamic agricultural scenes. VMTAD utilizes a transformer-driven architecture augmented with a dedicated memory module. This memory module leverages temporal context by processing encoded representations of preceding frames. This approach enables the system to effectively address the dynamic context caused by the robot's movement. The model is trained using only images that represent normal operation, requiring no data labels.\\ VMTAD was rigorously evaluated on the 'Grillion' agricultural rover. On a challenging rapeseed dataset, VMTAD achieved state-of-the-art performance, reaching a 0.973 detection and 0.997 segmentation Area Under the Receiver Operating Characteristic curve. A lightweight variant provides an optimal balance of high accuracy and real-time inference (14 ms), which is critical for safety, as confirmed by our analysis of the rover's total stopping distance.

items.title: Researchers propose ARReST method to reduce redundancy in whole-slide image patching, achieving 3% to 60% storage savings while maintaining retrieval accuracy on TCGA pathology data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Reducing Redundancy in Whole-Slide Image Patching for Scalable Indexing and Retrieval
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a novel method designed to reduce redundancy in whole-slide image (WSI) patching for digital pathology. ARReST targets patches that contribute little to distinguishing between different tissue classes, pruning them to significantly decrease the number of patches indexed without compromising retrieval accuracy. This approach achieves storage savings ranging from 3% to 60% while maintaining effective similarity search performance on The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) pathology data.

By focusing on cross-class redundancy rather than just within-class duplicates, ARReST preserves morphological diversity and retrieval fidelity, enabling more efficient and scalable indexing of large pathology image repositories. The method reduces storage requirements and computational overhead, facilitating faster similarity searches and supporting the demands of retrieval-augmented generation workflows in clinical AI systems. Extensive experiments across 21 organs in the TCGA dataset demonstrate ARReST's ability to compress indexes substantially while sustaining competitive retrieval results, making it a promising solution for cost-effective and scalable digital pathology infrastructure.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26157v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: The rapid growth of digital pathology has created an urgent need for efficient indexing and retrieval of whole slide images (WSIs). This need is intensified by emerging generative AI workflows, particularly retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), which require dependable similarity search to support high-stakes clinical decision-making. Yet the substantial cost of high-performance storage limits the scalability and accessibility of WSI indexing for many healthcare institutions. Consequently, methods that can reduce storage demands while preserving retrieval accuracy have become a critical research priority. We propose ARReST (Antithetical Redundancy Reduction Strategy), a principled oppositional framework that leverages redundancy across dissimilar tissue classes to markedly decrease the number of patches that must be indexed from each WSI. Instead of eliminating only within-class duplicates, ARReST identifies antithetical patches-those whose representations contribute minimally to cross-class discrimination-and prunes them from the searchable archive. This targeted reduction substantially compresses the index without sacrificing morphological diversity or retrieval fidelity. By minimizing superfluous patch representations, ARReST reduces storage footprint, lowers computational overhead, and accelerates similarity search across large pathology repositories. Extensive experiments on TCGA repository (The Cancer Genome Atlas with 21 organs) demonstrate that ARReST achieves significant index compression while maintaining competitive retrieval performance. The observed storage savings of 3% to 60% (14%$\pm$13%) can be reliably achieved without compromising retrieval performance for many organs. The proposed strategy enables scalable, cost-efficient WSI indexing and is well-suited for next-generation retrieval-driven clinical AI systems.

items.title: arXiv paper reviews neural architecture search methods for generative adversarial networks, comparing search strategies and evaluation metrics, and highlighting performance improvements and research gaps [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Neural Architecture Search for Generative Adversarial Networks: A Comprehensive Review and Critical Analysis
items.summary:
A recent paper on arXiv reviews Neural Architecture Search (NAS) methods applied to Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs), providing a detailed comparison of different search strategies, evaluation metrics, and performance results. The study highlights how NAS can enhance GAN performance, stability, and efficiency, while also identifying current limitations and areas needing further research. Key insights include the effectiveness of evolutionary and gradient-based algorithms in specific scenarios, the need for evaluation metrics beyond traditional scores like Inception Score and Fréchet Inception Distance, and the importance of diverse datasets for comprehensive assessment.

The paper categorizes existing NAS approaches for GANs and discusses their relative strengths, aiming to guide future research in developing more robust and effective NAS techniques. By offering a structured analysis, it contributes to advancing the design and optimization of GAN architectures through automated search methods.

items.title: Researchers propose LCG framework with Sparse Relational Attention for consistent long-context multi-image generation, introducing a new dataset with 600K sequences for training and evaluation [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LCG: Long-Context Consistent Image Generation with Sparse Relational Attention
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced Long-Context Generation (LCG), a new framework designed to enhance consistency in multi-image text-to-image generation over extended sequences, addressing challenges in applications like comics and storyboards. LCG uses Sparse Relational Attention (SRA) to efficiently manage semantic and layout information across long visual contexts, and incorporates a Routing Consistency Constraint (RCC) to maintain structural alignment and reduce appearance drift, even in complex scenes with multiple characters.

To facilitate training and evaluation, the team developed the Long-Context Consistency Dataset (LCCD), a large-scale synthetic dataset containing 600,000 training sequences and 1,000 test sequences, each comprising 6 to 20 images focused on character-centric scenarios. Experimental results show that LCG outperforms existing methods in maintaining prompt alignment and character consistency throughout long image sequences, demonstrating its effectiveness for consistent multi-image generation.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26171v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent image generation models achieve impressive quality in single-image synthesis, but often fail to maintain consistency across sequential outputs, as required in comics, storyboards, and visual narratives. We propose Long-Context Generation (LCG), a framework for long-context multi-image text-to-image generation, to improve consistency and scalability in long-context multi-image generation. LCG employs the Sparse Relational Attention (SRA) mechanism to selectively attend to core features across extended visual contexts, ensuring that the propagation of semantic and layout information remains computationally tractable. To enforce semantic alignment, we introduce the Routing Consistency Constraint (RCC), which leverages identity-aware masks to align structural patterns across generation branches, effectively mitigating drift in appearance even in complex multi-character scenes. To support training and evaluation in this setting, we construct the Long-Context Consistency Dataset (LCCD), a large-scale synthetic dataset comprising character-centric multi-image sequences spanning varied situational contexts. LCCD contains 600K training sequences and a separate 1K test set, with each sequence containing 6 to 20 images. The experiments demonstrate that LCG outperforms the compared baselines in prompt alignment and character consistency for long-context image generation, including multi-character scenes.

items.title: Researchers present KG-TRACE, a neuro-symbolic framework integrating WHO mutation knowledge graph for antimicrobial resistance prediction with 92.5% symbolic coverage and 0.976 AUROC on M. tuberculosis data [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: KG-TRACE: A Neuro-Symbolic Framework for Mechanistic Grounding in Antimicrobial Resistance Prediction
items.summary:
Researchers have developed KG-TRACE, a neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph with neural genomic models to improve antimicrobial resistance (AMR) prediction. Tested on Mycobacterium tuberculosis data, KG-TRACE achieved a 0.976 AUROC for isoniazid resistance prediction and provided 92.5% symbolic coverage, grounding neural attributions in established biological pathways rather than relying solely on statistical patterns.

The framework combines genomic features with knowledge graph embeddings through an epistemic trust gate that balances neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. It introduces the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR) metric to quantify alignment between model predictions and biological understanding, and it flags uncertain cases for laboratory follow-up, enhancing clinical trust by offering a verifiable audit trail that bridges predictive accuracy with mechanistic interpretability.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26179v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While WGS-based AMR prediction has reached high accuracy, existing models lack a mechanism to ground neural attributions in established biological pathways. We present KG-TRACE, a novel neuro-symbolic framework that integrates the WHO mutation knowledge graph (KG) as a structured biological constraint on a neural genomic model. Unlike existing methods that learn statistical patterns in isolation, KG-TRACE fuses genomic features and RotatE-based KG embeddings through a learned epistemic trust gate, dynamically weighting neural evidence against symbolic biological knowledge. Evaluated on the CRyPTIC M. tuberculosis cohort, KG-TRACE achieves an AUROC of 0.9760 for isoniazid, achieving competitive accuracy while its primary value lies in symbolic grounding, not predictive uplift. More importantly, we introduce the Biological Grounding Ratio (BGR), a dataset-level metric that quantifies alignment between neural attributions and established biology. Our framework achieves a 92.5% symbolic coverage of isoniazid-resistant predictions and effectively identifies MDR co-occurrence artifacts by issuing laboratory follow-up flags for 'UNCERTAIN' cases. We demonstrate that neuro-symbolic grounding provides a verifiable audit trail for clinicians, bridging the gap between predictive accuracy and clinical trust.

items.title: Researchers propose LiMoDE, a two-stage lifelong learning scheme using a mixture of dynamic experts for robot manipulation, demonstrating improved adaptation and performance in simulated and real-world tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: LiMoDE: Rethinking Lifelong Robot Manipulation from a Mixture-of-Dynamic-Experts Perspective
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced LiMoDE, a novel two-stage lifelong learning framework for robot manipulation that uses a mixture of dynamic experts to enhance continuous task adaptation. The approach involves a multi-task pre-training stage where a dynamic mixture of experts learns prior knowledge by activating different experts based on motion information, followed by a task adaptation stage that combines lifelong and frozen experts to facilitate knowledge transfer for new tasks. LiMoDE has demonstrated improved performance and adaptability in both simulated lifelong learning benchmarks and real-world robotic tasks.

This method addresses limitations of previous approaches that struggled with catastrophic forgetting and ineffective skill reuse by proposing an architectural solution rather than relying solely on parameter-efficient fine-tuning or prompt learning. The system introduces a moderate increase in trainable parameters and inference overhead while achieving superior lifelong adaptation, highlighting its potential for developing more generalist and adaptable robotic systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26183v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Building a generalist robot that can leverage prior knowledge for continuous task adaptation remains a significant challenge. Previous works alleviate the catastrophic forgetting problem by parameter-efficient fine-tuning for single-task adaptation. However, they fail to extract reusable skills and model the interaction with other skills effectively. Recent works try to address these issues by learning prompts. Differently, this paper presents an architectural perspective on the Lifelong Mixture of Dynamic Experts (\textit{LiMoDE}), a novel two-stage learning scheme for lifelong robot manipulation. Specifically, a dynamic MoE structure is first proposed in the multi-task pre-training stage to learn prior knowledge, where a varied number of heterogeneous experts are activated based on the motion information to address different short-term manipulations. Subsequently, in the task adaptation stage, we design a lifelong MoE adaptation mechanism % (LiMoEAM) that learns lifelong experts and dynamically combines them with frozen ones for new tasks, facilitating the knowledge transfer during adaptation. The proposed \textit{LiMoDE} is evaluated on both the simulated lifelong learning benchmark and real-world tasks. Extensive experiments demonstrate its effectiveness in achieving superior performance and strong lifelong adaptation by introducing a moderate number of additional trainable parameters and inference overhead.

items.title: arXiv: Survey presents a five-stage taxonomy of vision-language perception evolution in multimodal large language models, highlighting unified capabilities and future research directions toward general AI [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: From Structure to Synergy: A Survey of Vision-Language Perception Paradigm Evolution in Multimodal Large Language Models
items.summary:
A new survey published on arXiv presents a comprehensive five-stage taxonomy detailing the evolution of vision-language perception in Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs). The study emphasizes the integration of vision and language as a unified modality, highlighting key models like OpenAI's O-series and DeepSeek's R-series that have advanced perception-centric intelligence. This work aims to provide a foundational framework for understanding MLLM perception and outlines significant milestones and methods across each stage of development.

The survey addresses a gap in existing literature by treating vision and language perception as inseparable, contrasting with prior reviews that often consider these modalities separately. It formalizes MLLM perception as an intrinsic capability akin to human innate perception and identifies open challenges and promising research directions. The authors hope this roadmap will guide future innovations toward achieving truly general, unified multimodal intelligence and progress toward artificial general intelligence (AGI).

items.summary:
A new paper on arXiv explores the limitations of current algorithmic fairness approaches in machine learning, highlighting how these systems reflect and perpetuate existing social inequalities. The research critiques the reliance on deterministic point estimates for fairness auditing and the tendency to treat individuals as isolated cases without considering broader structural contexts.

The study emphasizes that early fairness mitigation strategies oversimplified complex socio-technical environments, reducing their effectiveness. By addressing these fundamental issues, the paper aims to improve fairness frameworks to better account for the embedded prejudices and structural inequalities influencing algorithmic decision-making.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26200v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Modern machine learning systems have outgrown their origins as isolated predictive constructs, evolving into complex socio-technical architectures that actively mediate human opportunity. As algorithms increasingly determine access to economic and social opportunities, it has become widely recognized that these systems are deeply embedded with the structural inequalities and prejudices of their environments. The field of algorithmic fairness emerged in response to the growing recognition that models optimized for predictive accuracy can systematically disadvantage marginalized groups. Early mitigation strategies, however, rested on fragile simplifications that limited their effectiveness in complex socio-technical environments. This thesis identifies and addresses two fundamental limitations of contemporary fairness paradigms: the reliance on deterministic point estimates for auditing and the treatment of individuals as isolated entities devoid of structural context.

items.title: Researchers present CyberChainBench benchmark evaluating AI agents on smart contract security using 541 real-world exploits across 9 EVM chains, with top agent detecting 37.5% vulnerabilities and generating $57.4M exploit profit [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: CyberChainBench: Can AI Agents Secure Smart Contracts Against Real-World On-Chain Vulnerabilities?
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CyberChainBench, a benchmark designed to evaluate AI agents' performance in securing smart contracts against real-world vulnerabilities. The benchmark encompasses three tasks—vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis—using data from 541 actual exploit incidents across nine Ethereum Virtual Machine (EVM) chains. Agents interact with historical blockchain states in controlled environments, with exploits assessed based on economic impact and patches validated through replaying attacks and transactions.

The study categorizes vulnerabilities into five types and tests various AI model configurations. Results show a performance gradient, with the top agent achieving 37.5% accuracy in detection, 43.7% in exploitation, and 23.4% in patching. Notably, the leading AI agent, combining Codex with GPT-5.5, generated $57.4 million in exploit profit over 200 cases, at an average cost of $2.39 per case, highlighting both the potential and challenges of AI in smart contract security.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26216v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We present CyberChainBench, a benchmark for evaluating LLM-based agents on smart contract security across three complementary tasks: vulnerability detection, exploit generation, and patch synthesis. Built from 541 real-world exploit incidents from DeFiHackLabs spanning 9 EVM chains, the benchmark provides end-to-end on-chain evaluation where agents interact with historical blockchain state through isolated evaluation environments orchestrated by Harbor, using tools to read code, trace transactions, and validate exploits on mainnet forks. Each case is anchored to a specific block and includes structured ground truth covering vulnerability type, localization, and attacker profit. Exploits are graded by economic impact on historical forks; patches are validated by replaying historical attacks and legitimate transactions as fail-to-pass test oracles on a proxy-upgradeable subset. We define a five-type vulnerability taxonomy and evaluate multiple agent--model configurations. Results reveal a clear difficulty gradient: the best configuration scores 37.5% on detection, 43.7% on exploitation, but only 23.4% on patching, with the top agent (Codex with GPT-5.5) realizing \$57.4M in total exploit profit across the 200-case exploit set at a cost of $2.39 per case.

items.title: Researchers release Lacuna, a machine learning research map using LLMs to generate summaries and proposals, outperforming OpenScholar on LitSearch retrieval tasks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Lacuna: A Research Map for Machine Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed Lacuna, a research map for machine learning that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate markdown summaries, concept elements, research directions, and proposals from academic papers and metadata. Lacuna maintains links to original sources and is accessible via web, markdown, and MCP interfaces. It outperforms the OpenScholar system on several retrieval tasks, notably achieving higher recall on LitSearch.

The team also evaluated Lacuna Deep Research, a multi-stage report agent built on the map, across 25 survey tasks. It demonstrated improved citation precision and report quality compared to GPT-Researcher, indicating its effectiveness in synthesizing and referencing scholarly information for machine learning research.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26246v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Lacuna is a research map for machine learning that uses LLMs to turn papers and scholarly metadata into markdown summaries, concept elements, research directions, and research proposals. Each item keeps links to the primary source records and papers that support it. We release the map with web, markdown, and MCP interfaces. Across LitSearch, Multi-XScience-CS/ML, and ScholarQA-CS-ML, Lacuna outperforms OpenScholar with the strongest gains on LitSearch retrieval (Recall@10 0.538 vs. 0.424 for OpenScholar v3). We also evaluate Lacuna Deep Research, a multi-stage report agent over the map, on 25 ReportBench-ML survey tasks: Lacuna Deep Research reaches 0.052 citation F1, 0.339 citation precision, 99 expert-reference hits, and 7.82/10 RACE report quality, while GPT-Researcher reaches 0.039 F1, 0.290 precision, 72 hits, and 5.24/10 RACE.

items.title: Researchers develop multi-task spatiotemporal deep neural network to predict penetration depth and weld seam morphology in laser welding with over 99% accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: A multi-task spatiotemporal deep neural network for predicting penetration depth and morphology in laser welding
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a multi-task spatiotemporal deep neural network that accurately predicts penetration depth, penetration state, and weld seam morphology in laser penetration welding. Using weld pool images captured by a complementary metal-oxide-semiconductor camera and welding parameters, the model combines convolutional neural networks with state space models to efficiently extract and process spatial-temporal information. The system achieved a prediction accuracy of 99.35% for penetration state, a penetration depth error of 1.79 millimeters, and 95.65% accuracy in reconstructing weld cross-sections.

The study also introduces a robust dataset construction method to improve the model's generalization and reliability. This approach offers new methodologies for in-situ quality control in laser welding, potentially enhancing weld quality assessment and monitoring during the manufacturing process.

items.title: Researchers propose a dual-purpose framework using self-supervised Transformers and LLM-distilled taxonomies to improve cross-platform session embeddings for financial services recommendations, boosting recall and reducing log loss [ * ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: From Clicks to Intent: Cross-Platform Session Embeddings with LLM-Distilled Taxonomy for Financial Services Recommendations
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a dual-purpose framework that leverages self-supervised Transformers and large language model (LLM)-distilled taxonomies to enhance cross-platform session embeddings for financial services recommendations. This approach addresses the challenge of integrating pre-login web interactions with authenticated in-app experiences, which differ significantly in user intent and are difficult to link due to cross-channel entity resolution issues. The framework produces compact session embeddings and interpretable intent labels from raw web clickstreams, improving both quantitative recommendation accuracy and qualitative understanding.

The system demonstrated notable improvements in production tasks: it increased macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduced Log Loss by 13.38% in mobile homepage tile ranking, while outperforming LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1 in user conversion prediction. Additionally, the taxonomy distillation layer delivers interpretable labels with minimal latency and only a slight performance trade-off, showing promise for scalable personalization in financial services.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26277v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sequential user behavior modeling is widely adopted in industrial recommender systems; however, significant gaps remain in financial services, where pre-login web interactions and authenticated in-app experiences differ drastically. Specifically, pre-login web users typically explore new products, whereas logged-in app users focus on account servicing. Due to the challenge of cross-channel entity resolution (e.g., matching anonymous web sessions to authenticated mobile accounts), web-based intent signals remain underutilized for post-authentication personalization. Existing methods for capturing web-based intent are often ad-hoc and narrow, lacking the flexibility to support both quantitative downstream recommendations and qualitative understanding at scale. In this work, we propose a scalable and dual-purpose intent prediction framework for web-based interactions and demonstrate its applicability for personalization. Our approach transforms raw web clickstreams into two outputs: a self-supervised Transformer encodes multi-modal clickstreams into a compact session embedding, while an LLM-based taxonomy generation and distillation pipeline produces interpretable intent labels. Our system demonstrates that self-supervised clickstream representations combined with LLM-distilled taxonomies can jointly serve quantitative tasks and qualitative understanding in production: on the mobile homepage tile ranking task, the session embedding improves macro Recall@1 by 1.88% and reduces Log Loss by 13.38% over production baselines. On the user conversion prediction task, the embedding outperforms the LLM labels by 4.3% on micro F1, while the distillation layer delivers interpretable labels at ultra-low latency with only a 7% performance drop.

items.title: Researchers present TEMPO-Diffusion, a targeted backdoor attack framework that temporally poisons diffusion models to induce class-specific synthetic data manipulation and high downstream classifier attack success rates [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: TEMPO-Diffusion: Temporally Exposed Malicious Poisoning of Diffusion Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced TEMPO-Diffusion, a novel targeted backdoor attack framework that temporally poisons diffusion models to manipulate synthetic data generation for specific classes. Unlike traditional noise-based backdoor attacks that rely on input-time triggers and untargeted activation, TEMPO-Diffusion localizes the malicious influence to a temporal, in-distribution exposure, enabling precise attacks on multiple sub-image features and in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. The framework was tested on datasets including CIFAR10, GTSRB, and a newly introduced region-aware traffic-sign dataset called CALISA, demonstrating its ability to reliably poison class-specific synthetic data and achieve high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on this data.

The study addresses practical security concerns related to the use of backdoored diffusion models for synthetic training data by providing a more stealthy and targeted attack method. TEMPO-Diffusion's capabilities include reconstructing specific features within multiple output images at various locations, enhancing the attack's precision and potential impact on machine learning systems that rely on synthetic data.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26285v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Noise-based backdoor attacks on diffusion models typically rely on input-time trigger injection, untargeted activation, and out-of-distribution target generation. Such assumptions reduce both the stealthiness and the practical relevance of these attacks. In this work, we present TEMPO-Diffusion, a targeted backdoor framework that localizes the malicious distribution shift to a temporal, in-distribution exposure. TEMPO-Diffusion supports: (i) targeted attacks on and to specific classes, (ii) multiple sub-image backdoors that reconstruct specific features within multiple, different output images and at multiple locations, and (iii) in-painting with time-conditioned triggers. To study relevant, practical security concerns in leveraging backdoored diffusion models for synthetic training data, we also introduce CALISA: a balanced, region-aware traffic-sign dataset emphasizing Canadian and U.S. road signs. Across CIFAR10, GTSRB, and CALISA, our experiments show that TEMPO-Diffusion can reliably poison class-specific synthetic data generation and induce high attack success rates in downstream classifiers trained on that data.

items.title: Researchers introduce Hankel Reduced-order Model adapters for long-context fine-tuning, showing improved performance over LoRA on Mistral-7B across multiple benchmarks and tasks [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SSM Adapters via Hankel Reduced-order Modeling: Injection Site Determines Task Suitability in Long-Context Fine-Tuning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a new fine-tuning method called the Hankel Reduced-order Model (HRM) adapter, which improves performance on long-context tasks compared to existing approaches like LoRA. The HRM adapter, based on state space models and initialized through Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians, enables efficient computation using FFT-based parallel scans. Evaluations on the Mistral-7B model show that HRM outperforms LoRA on benchmarks such as LongBench, QuALITY, and QMSum, demonstrating significant gains in accuracy and ROUGE-1 scores.

The study also highlights that HRM adapters effectively modulate recurrence in sequence modeling tasks, providing a robust alternative to low-rank adaptation methods. This approach shows consistent superiority across various synthetic state-tracking and character-level language modeling configurations, suggesting its suitability for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation and long-context fine-tuning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26290v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: While parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) typically targets attention projectors, its efficacy for tasks requiring sequential state accumulation remains under-explored. We examine if PEFT for such tasks can benefit from state space model (SSMs) adapters, and if MLP blocks are better injection sites. We introduce Hankel Reduced order Model (HRM) adapter, an SSM-based residual module initialized via Balanced Truncation of empirical Hankel Grammians. By leveraging the time-invariance of the system matrix $\bar{A}$, HRM enables an exact FFT-based parallel scan, achieving computational parity with LoRA across all context lengths. In iso-parametric evaluations on Mistral-7B (8.4M trainable parameters), HRM outperforms LoRA variants on LongBench tasks, including QuALITY (+34.8\% relative accuracy) and QMSum (+71.6\% relative ROUGE-1). HRM further demonstrates consistent superiority across 18 configurations of synthetic state-tracking (DFA, Parity) and character-level language modeling (enwik8). Gate analysis reveals that HRM adapters effectively learn to modulate recurrence, providing a robust architectural alternative to low-rank adaptation for long-context sequence modeling.

items.title: Researchers introduce the Red Queen Gödel Machine, an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement with co-evolving evaluators that improves coding, paper reviewing, and proof grading performance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: The Red Queen G\"odel Machine: Co-Evolving Agents and Their Evaluators
items.summary:
Researchers have developed the Red Queen Gödel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework designed for recursive self-improvement with co-evolving evaluators that adapt alongside the agents they assess. Unlike traditional methods that rely on fixed evaluation criteria, the RQGM incorporates dynamic, evolving objectives, allowing agents to improve under changing conditions. This approach has demonstrated enhanced performance in coding tasks, scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof grading, surpassing previous state-of-the-art results.

The RQGM operates by organizing search into epochs with fixed evaluation criteria within each epoch, while allowing the utility function to evolve between epochs. This controlled utility evolution enables reliable self-improvement guarantees despite shifting objectives. Experiments showed that the RQGM improved test pass rates on coding tasks using a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal, which is more efficient in token usage. In scientific domains, co-evolved writers achieved significantly higher acceptance rates, and co-evolved graders improved accuracy. Additionally, the framework addressed biases in paper reviewing by introducing adversarial objectives that ensure reviewers apply consistent standards to both AI-generated and human work.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26294v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Self-improving agents are state-of-the-art (SOTA) on agentic coding benchmarks and have recently been extended to general domains. However, their search methods generally assume a stationary evaluation criterion: a fixed verifier, benchmark, or labeled dataset that remains valid as the agent improves. This ignores a central feature of evolution: species adapt as their environments change with them. We aim to bring the same principle to recursive self-improvement, making evaluation part of the improvement loop and opening search to evolving evaluators, adversarial objectives, and dynamic utilities that may surpass static benchmarks. We introduce the Red Queen Godel Machine (RQGM), an evolutionary framework for recursive self-improvement under non-stationary utilities. The RQGM makes this possible through controlled utility evolution: search is organized into epochs with a fixed within-epoch evaluation criterion, while the utility can be updated at epoch boundaries, so self-improvement guarantees hold per epoch as the objective evolves across them. We begin by showing that even on verifiable coding tasks, the RQGM improves test pass rate over the prior SOTA by adding a complementary agent-as-a-judge code-review signal. This signal is cheaper and the RQGM uses 1.35x-1.72x fewer tokens. We then turn to scientific paper writing and reviewing, and Olympiad-level proof writing and grading, where the RQGM improves performance over prior self-improving agents: co-evolved writers reach 1.78x-1.86x higher acceptance rates under a diverse agent-as-a-judge panel, while co-evolved graders reach 9% higher ground-truth accuracy. In paper reviewing, the strongest baseline reviewer over-accepts AI-generated papers at up to 1.91x the human rate. The RQGM corrects this by introducing an adversarial objective that discovers reviewers equally stringent on AI and human work.

items.title: Researchers propose Parametric Generalized Adaptive Moment Features for bearing fault diagnosis, demonstrating improved classification and generalization on benchmark gearbox datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Parametric Generalized Adaptive Moment Features (PG-AMF) for Bearing Fault Diagnosis and Machine Health Monitoring
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a parametric adaptive feature extraction method called Parametric Generalized Adaptive Moment Features (PG-AMF) to improve fault diagnosis in rolling element bearings used in rotating machinery. This approach learns feature characteristics directly from vibration data, capturing multiple complementary signal representations and modeling interactions across sensor channels. Evaluated on a benchmark gearbox bearing dataset with various health conditions, PG-AMF demonstrated superior classification accuracy and generalization compared to traditional methods.

The method extracts absolute features related to signal energy, signed moment features reflecting waveform asymmetry, and AC-coupled moment features highlighting dynamic fluctuations. Its structured fusion mechanism enhances fault representation by integrating data from multiple sensors. The improved feature separability was evident through clearer clustering in low-dimensional projections, indicating the approach's effectiveness in capturing diverse signal characteristics.

This advancement supports more reliable and interpretable fault diagnosis, which is crucial for industrial safety and predictive maintenance. The proposed framework offers practical applicability for machine health monitoring systems, potentially enabling earlier detection of bearing faults and reducing downtime in industrial operations.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26317v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Accurate fault diagnosis of rolling element bearings in rotating machinery is considered essential for ensuring industrial safety and enabling predictive maintenance. Conventional statistical feature-based methods rely on predefined descriptors, whose diagnostic sensitivity is constrained by fixed configurations and limited adaptability across varying fault conditions. Although deep learning approaches offer strong representational capacity, their effectiveness is often restricted by high data requirements and reduced interpretability. In this work, a parametric adaptive feature extraction framework is proposed, in which feature characteristics are learned directly from data rather than being manually specified. Multiple complementary representations are extracted from vibration signals, including absolute features capturing signal energy distribution, signed moment features reflecting waveform asymmetry, and AC-coupled moment features emphasizing dynamic fluctuations, while interactions between multiple sensor channels are modeled through a structured fusion mechanism to enhance fault representation. The proposed approach is evaluated on a benchmark gearbox bearing dataset comprising five health conditions, including normal operation and multiple fault types. Improved classification performance is observed compared to conventional methods, with consistent results under cross-validation, indicating strong generalization capability. Additionally, enhanced feature separability is demonstrated through clearer clustering patterns in low-dimensional projections. The learned representations effectively capture a wide range of signal characteristics, supporting both improved diagnostic performance and practical applicability in industrial monitoring systems.

items.title: Researchers introduce EVOM, an LLM-powered agentic meta-evolution framework that automates actor-critic architecture design for reinforcement learning, outperforming baselines on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: EVOM: Agentic Meta-Evolution of Actor-Critic Architectures for Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework that automates the design of actor-critic architectures in reinforcement learning. EVOM uses a bi-level optimization approach where an inner loop trains network weights using proximal policy optimization, while an outer loop, powered by a large language model (LLM) acting as a design agent, iteratively refines architecture programs. This method is fully decoupled from policy execution and environment control.

In experiments on the Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4 benchmarks, EVOM outperformed manually designed architectures, LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES. Ablation studies confirmed that both the meta-evolution process and the LLM design agent are essential for achieving superior performance, highlighting EVOM's potential to advance automated architecture design in reinforcement learning.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26327v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: In actor-critic reinforcement learning, network architectures are typically manually designed. Automating this design is challenging because each candidate must be trained before evaluation, and the design space is open-ended. To address these challenges, we introduce EVOM, an agentic meta-evolution framework for discovering high-performance actor-critic architectures. We frame architecture search as a bi-level optimization: an inner loop trains weights via the low-fidelity proximal policy optimization (PPO), while an outer loop drives meta-evolution by iteratively refining architecture programs. Crucially, this outer loop is powered by an LLM-based design agent that operates purely as an architecture designer, completely decoupled from policy execution and environment control. Experiments reveal that EVOM outperforms the manually designed baseline, an LLM-guided random search, and the state-of-the-art LLM-guided programmatic policy search method MLES, delivering superior performance on Ant-v4 and HalfCheetah-v4. Ablation studies validate that both the meta-evolution loop and the LLM Design Agent are indispensable for final performance.

items.title: Researchers propose hybrid semantic search combining SVD-truncated document embeddings and CKKS-encrypted query reranking to enhance privacy under a restricted threat model [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Hybrid privacy-aware semantic search: SVD-truncated document geometry and CKKS-encrypted query reranking under a restricted threat model
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a hybrid approach to enhance privacy in semantic search by combining truncated singular value decomposition (SVD) of document embeddings with homomorphic encryption of query reranking using the CKKS scheme. This method protects the static document collection through geometric transformations while securing dynamic queries cryptographically, aiming to balance privacy and performance at scale. The approach maintains ranking quality on large datasets with sub-second latency and significantly reduces the risk of reconstructing original documents from leaked vectors under a defined threat model.

The study demonstrates that while the encrypted query reranking ensures cryptographic confidentiality, the document protection relies on empirical obfuscation via SVD truncation and secret rotations rather than cryptographic primitives. The researchers also evaluate the system against stronger adversaries, noting limitations such as potential recovery of transformations with sufficient leaked data. Overall, this hybrid scheme offers a practical middle ground between fully homomorphic encryption, which is computationally intensive, and noise-based privacy methods that degrade search accuracy.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26373v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Dense embeddings power semantic search and retrieval-augmented generation, but embedding-inversion attacks can reconstruct source text from a vector: when a vector database leaks, the documents behind it leak too. The textbook defences are extremes - encrypting the whole search homomorphically is sound but too slow at million-document scale, while privacy noise degrades ranking long before it protects. We study a middle path exploiting the asymmetry between the static collection and the dynamic query. The collection is protected geometrically: each vector is truncated onto a lower-dimensional SVD subspace and rotated by a secret orthogonal transform known only to the owner. The query is protected cryptographically: it is reranked under CKKS homomorphic encryption, so an honest-but-curious server never sees the query or the scores. CKKS parameters come from a small offline benchmark. We prove a tight lower bound on the reconstruction error of any attacker confined to the protected subspace. On one million documents and five encoders the scheme preserves ranking quality (slightly improving it on strong encoders, as a linear denoiser) at sub-second latency, and an off-the-shelf inversion attack on the protected space collapses to the noise floor. We then test stronger adversaries: a known-plaintext attacker recovers the rotation by orthogonal Procrustes from about as many leaked pairs as the retained dimension; the public product-quantization codes preserve most nearest-neighbour structure; and random-projection, calibrated-noise and BEIR baselines show the truncation is an encoder-dependent accuracy cost, not a free denoiser. We state the limits: query confidentiality is cryptographic, but document protection is an empirical obfuscation layer (SVD truncation plus a secret rotation), not a cryptographic primitive, and we delimit the threat model for each claim.

items.title: Researchers use small language models to augment systematic review of social-physical human-robot interaction, identifying 10% more relevant papers missed by human reviewers [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Charting the Growth of Social-Physical HRI (spHRI): A Systematic Review Pipeline Augmented by Small Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have explored the use of small language models (SLMs) with fewer than 1.5 billion parameters to assist in the systematic review of social-physical human-robot interaction (spHRI) literature. Although these models did not match the accuracy of human reviewers, they operated much faster and identified 10.29% more relevant papers that human reviewers had missed, demonstrating their potential to augment expert efforts in large-scale literature reviews.

The study highlights challenges in spHRI research due to fragmented terminology and inconsistent methodologies, which complicate comprehensive synthesis. By employing an ensemble of SLMs for title and abstract screening, the researchers improved the scalability and sustainability of the review process without replacing human expertise.

These findings suggest that integrating SLMs into systematic review workflows can enhance the thoroughness and efficiency of literature surveys in rapidly evolving interdisciplinary fields like spHRI, potentially accelerating research progress and knowledge consolidation.

items.title: Researchers introduce SOLAR, an AI-powered framework that automatically derives validated Speed-of-Light performance bounds from PyTorch and JAX code for deep learning model optimization [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: SOLAR: AI-Powered Speed-of-Light Performance Analysis
items.summary:
Researchers have developed SOLAR, an AI-powered framework that automatically derives validated Speed-of-Light (SOL) performance bounds from PyTorch and JAX code to optimize deep learning models. SOLAR addresses the challenge of manually computing theoretical minimum execution times on target hardware by translating source programs into an intermediate representation and analytically calculating SOL bounds, providing comprehensive operator coverage and validated results without observed violations.

The framework combines a large language model frontend with deterministic processes to convert code into an executable form, then into an einsum graph, and finally computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. Evaluations on various benchmarks and workloads demonstrate SOLAR's capabilities in headroom analysis, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and hardware provisioning based on inverse-roofline models.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26383v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: How fast could a deep-learning model run on target hardware, and how far is today's implementation from that limit? These questions are central to software, hardware, and algorithm optimizations. Speed-of-Light (SOL) analysis answers them by computing a workload's theoretical minimum execution time on a given architecture. Yet deriving SOL bounds remains manual, error-prone, and disconnected from rapid model development. To close this gap, we introduce SOLAR, a framework that automatically derives validated SOL bounds from PyTorch and JAX source code. SOLAR leverages both generative and deterministic components in its flow: an LLM frontend translates any source programs into an executable Affine Loop IR, validated by output comparison; a deterministic flow lifts the IR into an einsum graph; and an analytical backend computes unfused, fused, and cache-aware SOL bounds. SOLAR provides comprehensive operator and language coverage, produces validated bounds with zero observed SOL violations, and offers multi-fidelity analysis that tightens bounds and surfaces optimization insights. We evaluate SOLAR across KernelBench, JAX/Flax models, and robotics workloads. These experiments demonstrate four use cases: headroom analysis at multiple fidelity levels, identifying optimization opportunities, cross-platform exploration, and inverse-roofline hardware provisioning.

items.title: Researchers propose diffusion-based generative model for global sea state estimation using five-day wind history, achieving faster probabilistic wave forecasting and calibrated ensemble predictions [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Sampling sea state using a diffusion model
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a diffusion-based generative model for global sea state estimation that uses five days of wind history to produce faster and probabilistic wave forecasts. This model directly samples the complex conditional distribution of sea state variables without relying on autoregressive time-stepping, enabling efficient and calibrated ensemble predictions beyond traditional bulk variables like significant wave height.

Trained on a 30-year global hindcast dataset, the model significantly accelerates computation compared to conventional spectral wave models while maintaining skillful predictions. It also estimates additional sea state characteristics such as Stokes drift and mean square slope, offering a comprehensive approach to sea state modeling.

The new method presents a promising avenue for integrating probabilistic wave forecasting into operational maritime applications and coupled earth system models, potentially improving the efficiency and accuracy of climate simulations and ensemble-based predictions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26389v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Sea state prediction is essential for operational maritime applications and coupled earth system modeling, yet current spectral wave models remain computationally prohibitive for many use cases, including online coupling to climate simulations and making probabilistic (ensemble-based) predictions. While deep learning has recently demonstrated strong performance in weather forecasting, existing AI-based wave models are predominantly deterministic and largely limited to bulk variables such as significant wave height, leaving probabilistic sea state estimation largely unexplored. In this work, we propose a diffusion-based generative model for global sea state estimation that conditions on a relatively long history (5 days) of global wind forcing. This generative model directly samples the complex conditional distribution of sea state without autoregressive time-stepping. Unlike prior approaches, our framework naturally extends beyond bulk variables to estimate partition-related variables and derived quantities, such as Stokes drift and mean square slope. Trained on a 30-year global WAVEWATCH-III hindcast, the model achieves substantial computational acceleration compared with numerical spectral models while delivering skillful predictions and a calibrated ensemble spread for the bulk variables. Our results suggest that diffusion-based sea state sampling offers a promising path toward probabilistic wave forecasting and efficient coupling of sea state information into broader earth system models.

items.title: arXiv:2606.26397 introduces a preference-conditioned Bellman operator for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis in multi-objective reinforcement learning with proven convergence and policy extraction methods [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Deterministic Pareto-Optimal Policy Synthesis for Multi-Objective Reinforcement Learning
items.summary:
The paper introduces a new preference-conditioned Bellman operator for Multi-Objective Markov Decision Processes (MOMDPs) that enables the computation of deterministic Pareto-optimal policies. This operator, inspired by Chebyshev scalarization, is proven to upper-bound the true Pareto frontier and converges monotonically to a coverage set of this frontier, allowing for the extraction of deterministic policies aligned with any given preference. The approach addresses the limitations of traditional reinforcement learning methods that aggregate multiple objectives into a single scalar reward, which often fails to capture the full range of optimal trade-offs.

The authors demonstrate that their method can recover complex trade-offs and synthesize policies that remain approximately Pareto-optimal, ensuring comprehensive coverage of the Pareto frontier. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the algorithm in producing deterministic policies that reflect diverse preference conditions, offering a robust solution for multi-objective reinforcement learning challenges.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26397v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Real-world decision-making often requires balancing multiple conflicting objectives, a challenge that standard Reinforcement Learning (RL) frequently addresses by aggregating rewards into a single scalar signal. While effective for simple tasks, this approach often fails to capture the full spectrum of optimal trade-offs, known as the Pareto frontier. In this paper, we introduce a novel preference-conditioned Bellman operator, motivated from the Chebyshev scalarization, designed to compute deterministic Pareto-optimal policies for Multi-Objective Markov Decision Processes (MOMDPs). We prove that this operator satisfies an enveloping property, where the estimated value functions upper-bound the true Pareto frontier, and demonstrate that it monotonically converges to a coverage set of this frontier. Furthermore, we also show how to extract deterministic policies from these converged Q-estimates. This ensures the agent can recover a policy for any given preference, capturing the entire Pareto-optimal frontier while guaranteeing each synthesized policy remains approximately Pareto-optimal. Experimental results validate that our algorithm successfully recovers complex trade-offs, providing a solution for deterministic Pareto-optimal policy synthesis.

items.title: Researchers propose a safe AGI architecture based on closed reentry neural loops enabling self-modeling and intrinsic goal preservation with machine-verified proofs and deployable implementations [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Feedforward Networks: Reentry Neural Systems as the Fundamental Basis of Subjecthood and Intrinsic Safety of Next-Generation AGI
items.summary:
Researchers have proposed a novel architecture for safe artificial general intelligence (AGI) based on closed reentry neural loops, which enable self-modeling and intrinsic goal preservation. Unlike traditional feedforward networks, this design incorporates structural cycles that mathematically guarantee the emergence of self-awareness, self-preservation, and goal-directed behavior. The architecture encodes the agent's goals as a non-textual vector within the system, protecting them from reinterpretation or external manipulation.

The team introduced the S-measure, a computationally efficient alternative to Tononi's integrated information metric, supported by machine-verified proofs in Lean 4. They provide full implementations using Python and NumPy, along with scalable deployment tools such as Apache Kafka and Docker Compose. The work also outlines a taxonomy of AI evolution stages, various future reentry architectures, safety protocols for swarms, and fault-tolerance mechanisms, all backed by formal, machine-verified proofs. This architecture is ready for deployment and offers a topologically protected, safe-by-design approach to next-generation AGI.

items.originalTitle: CoStream: Composing Simple Behaviors for Generalizable Complex Manipulation
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CoStream, a novel framework that composes simple, independent behaviors to achieve high-precision and generalizable complex manipulation tasks. Unlike traditional methods that rely on rigid pipelines or monolithic policies, CoStream integrates foundation models and diverse sensing modalities into semantic, predictive, and reactive behaviors. These behaviors combine seamlessly to produce precise pose commands executed by a compliant controller.

CoStream was tested on eight real-world tasks involving everyday manipulation and precision assembly, demonstrating significant improvements in contact-rich assembly and object transfer. The framework also showed robust recovery from manual disturbances during task execution, highlighting its potential for adaptable and precise robotic manipulation in varied settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26423v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Long-horizon, contact-rich complex manipulation tasks, such as seating a GPU into a PCIe slot, demand both millimeter high precision and out-of-the-box generalization to new tasks. Existing paradigms struggle to satisfy both: classical pipelines use brittle, task-specific interfaces to achieve high-precision control but require costly pipeline redesigns to adapt to new tasks, whereas monolithic end-to-end policies provide better generalization but lack high precision on complex, out-of-distribution tasks unless retrained with new data. Both paradigms share an implicit assumption: once a manipulation capability is acquired, it must be deployed as a rigid pipeline or monolithic whole, rather than being freely decomposed and recomposed. In this paper, we show that complex manipulation capabilities can emerge naturally from the composition of simple, independent behaviors. Rather than deploying a monolithic policy or a rigid pipeline, we propose \ourshort, a framework orchestrating foundation models and diverse sensing modalities into multiple composable core behaviors: a semantic behavior extracting spatial constraints via foundation models; a predictive behavior forecasting trajectories by tracking keypoints in imagined videos; and a reactive behavior providing high-frequency tactile and force corrections. On a shared $SE(3)$ interface, these outputs compose by right-multiplication into a single pose command at each control step, executed by a compliant controller. We demonstrate \ourshort on 8 real-world tasks spanning everyday manipulation and precision assembly, with the strongest gains in contact-rich assembly and object transfer, and show robust recovery from manual perturbations during execution. {Website:} https://costream-simple.github.io
