items.title: Researchers propose In-Context Model Predictive Generation framework combining large language models and physical simulation for open-vocabulary human motion synthesis with improved realism and semantic fidelity [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: In-Context Model Predictive Generation: Open-Vocabulary Motion Synthesis from Language Models to Physics
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the In-Context Model Predictive Generation (ICMPG) framework, which combines large language models (LLMs) with physical simulation to synthesize human motion from textual descriptions. This approach addresses the challenge of balancing semantic accuracy and physical realism by integrating language-based planning with real-time physical feedback, enabling more realistic and semantically faithful motion generation without requiring task-specific retraining.

ICMPG operates through two modules: the Context-Aware Motion Generation (CAMG) module, which uses an LLM to interpret and decompose text commands into candidate motion sequences, and the Model Predictive Generation (MPG) module, which evaluates these sequences via physical simulation and semantic alignment to select the best motion. Extensive testing shows that ICMPG generalizes well to diverse and novel commands, outperforming existing methods in producing motions that adhere to both physical constraints and detailed semantic instructions.

This framework bridges the gap between semantic interpretation and physical simulation, offering flexibility to incorporate various LLM backbones. Its closed-loop refinement process enhances the versatility and control of text-driven human motion synthesis, promising improvements for immersive digital applications.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26981v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Synthesizing human motion from textual descriptions is essential for immersive digital applications, yet existing methods face a persistent trade-off between semantic fidelity and physical realism. Large language model (LLM)-based approaches can interpret diverse open-vocabulary instructions and compose high-level action plans, but they often generate motions that violate physical constraints. Physics-aware models improve realism through simulation or control, but they struggle with semantic complexity, fine-grained instructions, and novel concepts. To address this gap, we propose In-Context Model Predictive Generation (ICMPG), a framework that integrates language-model planning with inference-time physical feedback. ICMPG reformulates motion synthesis as a Model Predictive Control (MPC)-like process with two modules. The Context-Aware Motion Generation (CAMG) module uses an LLM as a planner to decompose textual commands and generate candidate motion sequences from motion tokens. The Model Predictive Generation (MPG) module evaluates these candidates through physical simulation and semantic alignment, estimates a composite reward, and selects the best sequence to guide subsequent generation steps. Unlike open-loop generation, this closed-loop refinement enables ICMPG to adapt motions to both the input semantics and the simulated physical environment without task-specific policy retraining. Extensive experiments across standard and zero-shot open-vocabulary settings show that ICMPG generalizes robustly to diverse commands and produces motions that are more physically plausible and semantically faithful than representative baselines on the evaluated benchmarks. The framework bridges semantic interpretation and physical simulation while remaining flexible enough to incorporate different LLM backbones, enabling more versatile and controllable text-driven motion synthesis.

items.title: Researchers analyze framing-sensitive behavioral variability in large language models across architectures, highlighting implications for mental health AI interaction consistency and trustworthiness [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Auditing Framing-Sensitive Behavioral Instability in Large Language Models for Mental Health Interactions
items.summary:
Researchers have examined how large language models (LLMs), increasingly used in mental health support and sensitive conversational applications, respond inconsistently to semantically similar inputs framed differently. This framing-sensitive variability poses challenges for ensuring stable and trustworthy AI behavior in psychological contexts. The study analyzed multiple instruction-tuned LLM architectures using controlled prompts and found that framing systematically influences model responses, with internal representations reflecting these variations across transformer layers.

Layer-wise probing revealed that behavior-related information remains decodable throughout the models, though decoding strength varies by architecture. Experiments also showed that certain representational directions linked to framing can partially steer model behavior. These findings highlight the importance of robustness to contextual framing when assessing the reliability and consistency of conversational AI systems deployed in mental health settings.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26982v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly being integrated into mental health support tools and other psychologically sensitive conversational applications. In such settings, behavioral stability and consistency are important for trustworthy human-AI interaction. However, semantically similar concerns can be presented through different contextual framings, potentially eliciting different model responses. Such framing-sensitive variability may challenge user expectations regarding system behavior and complicate the assessment of AI reliability. While prior studies have primarily examined such effects at the behavioral level, less is known about how framing-related variation is reflected in the internal representations of aligned language models. In this work, we investigate these effects using controlled matched prompts spanning multiple contextual framing conditions across several instruction-tuned model families. Across architectures, framing systematically alters interpretive response tendencies. Layer-wise probing analyses show that behavior-associated information remains decodable throughout transformer depth, with architecture-dependent variation in decoding strength. Moreover, held-out framing probes remained consistently above chance across architectures despite strong lexical baselines. Activation steering experiments further suggest that framing-associated representational directions can partially modulate downstream behavioral outcomes. Finally, these findings indicate that robustness to contextual variation may represent an important consideration when evaluating the consistency and trustworthiness of conversational AI systems deployed in mental-health-oriented interactions.

items.title: Researchers propose ReaORE, a reasoning-guided progressive framework for Open Relation Extraction using large reasoning models, outperforming baselines on two datasets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: ReaORE: Reasoning-Guided Progressive Open Relation Extraction Empowered by Large Reasoning Models
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced ReaORE, a reasoning-guided progressive framework designed to improve Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) by effectively identifying unseen relations between entities in unstructured text. ReaORE addresses limitations of existing methods by employing a two-stage process: relation filtering through multi-aspect reasoning and embedding-based similarity, followed by fine-grained comparative reasoning for precise relation prediction. This approach enables better generalization and distinction of closely related relations compared to previous clustering or direct label generation techniques.

Extensive testing on two widely used OpenRE datasets shows that ReaORE outperforms current baseline models, demonstrating its effectiveness in extracting accurate relation labels in real-world applications. The framework leverages large reasoning models to progressively refine relation extraction, enhancing both reliability and discriminative capacity in handling diverse and unseen relation types.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26986v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open Relation Extraction (OpenRE) requires a model to extract unseen relations between head and tail entities from unstructured text for real-world applications. The core challenge of OpenRE lies in achieving reliable generalization to unseen relation types. Current OpenRE approaches either employ clustering techniques, which cannot generate relation labels and suffer from poor generalization, or rely on direct relation label generation via Large Language Models (LLMs), which lack sufficient discriminative capacity to distinguish easily confused relations. To address these limitations, we propose Reasoning-guided progressive OpenRE (ReaORE), a framework for performing relation extraction through coarse-to-fine relation reasoning. Specifically, ReaORE consists of two key stages: (i) relation filtering, which reasons over multiple aspects to understand relations and instances, yielding an initial relation set, and further supplements and filters relations via embedding-based similarity to ensure the target relation is included; (ii) relation prediction, which aims to predict the target relations from the above set via fine-grained comparative reasoning to better distinguish easily confused relations. Extensive experiments on two widely used OpenRE datasets demonstrate that ReaORE outperforms existing baselines.

items.title: Researchers identify and compare emotion vectors encoding valence and arousal in two open-source LLMs, revealing differences in layer-wise representation and corpus sensitivity [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Where Do Models Find Happiness? Emotion Vectors in Open-Source LLMs
items.summary:
Researchers have identified and compared emotion vectors that encode valence and arousal in two open-source large language models, Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it. Their study reveals that while both models exhibit valence geometry similar to previous findings in Claude Sonnet 4.5, the way valence representations develop across model layers differs significantly between them. Additionally, arousal encoding varies depending on the corpus used for extraction, indicating that emotional cues are unevenly distributed in generated texts.

The team extracted emotion contrast vectors across all layers using two model-generated corpora and found that Gemma-4-E4B-it encodes valence strongly in early layers but loses it in later layers, whereas Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 shows the opposite pattern. Arousal alignment was stronger with stories generated by Gemma than those by Apertus, suggesting corpus sensitivity in arousal representation. The researchers have open-sourced their experiment code and dataset to support reproducible investigation of emotion representations across language model architectures.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26987v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Recent work identified emotion vectors in Claude Sonnet 4.5, which are internal representations that encode emotion concepts, causally influence behavior, and exhibit geometry mirroring human psychological structure. We test the generality of these findings in two open-weight models, Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 and Gemma-4-E4B-it, extracting emotion contrast vectors across all layers, using two model-generated corpora. We recover valence geometry for both models, with peak PC1--valence correlations of $r = 0.76$ and $r = 0.83$, approaching the $r = 0.81$ reported for Claude.Beyond replication, we observe notable differences in how valence representations emerge across model depth. In Gemma-4-E4B-it, valence is strongly encoded in early layers but collapses towards later layers, whereas Apertus-8B-Instruct-2509 exhibits the opposite pattern, with valence representations absent in early layers, but emerging at mid depths. Arousal encoding, in contrast, is sensitive to the extraction corpus: both models show stronger PC2--arousal alignment with Gemma-generated stories ($r$ up to $0.45$) than Apertus-generated ones ($r \leq 0.21$), suggesting arousal-relevant cues are unevenly distributed across generated corpora. We open-source our experiment code and dataset for reproducible investigation of emotion representations across language model architectures.

items.title: Researchers propose decision-aligned evaluation metrics for uncertainty quantification in machine learning, revealing misalignment in common metrics and introducing prior-weighted utility metrics for improved decision relevance [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Decision-Aligned Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification
items.summary:
Researchers have identified that common metrics used to evaluate uncertainty estimates in machine learning, such as negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error, often do not align well with the actual utility of decisions made based on these estimates. They introduce the concept of decision-alignment to assess which evaluation metrics correspond meaningfully to downstream decision-making outcomes. Their analysis reveals that many widely used metrics either misalign with typical decision problems or reflect unrealistic prior assumptions about tasks.

To address this, the researchers propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a new class of proper scoring rules designed to provide evaluation that aligns with decision utility. Through benchmark experiments and real-world case studies, these metrics consistently correlate with realized decision benefits, unlike conventional metrics. This work highlights limitations in current uncertainty quantification evaluation practices and offers a principled approach to improve the relevance of such evaluations for practical decision-making.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26990v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Uncertainty estimates in machine learning are typically evaluated using generic metrics such as the negative log-likelihood and expected calibration error, yet good performance on such metrics does not necessarily imply high utility in downstream decisions. We introduce decision-alignment, a criterion that reveals which evaluation metrics meaningfully align with downstream utilities. Applying this framework, we show that many widely used uncertainty metrics are either misaligned with common decision problems or encode pathological prior beliefs about the downstream task. We then propose prior-weighted utility metrics, a special class of proper scoring rules that provides decision-aligned uncertainty evaluation. Across benchmark experiments and real-world case studies, our metrics consistently align with realized decision utility, while conventional metrics do not. Our results surface flaws in the current UQ evaluation protocol and offer a principled extension of existing metrics toward decision-relevant UQ evaluation.

items.title: Researchers propose EVIS, an event-aware video instructed segmentation assistant using text-guided event queries and object-pixel-hybrid learning to improve referring video segmentation across five benchmarks [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Event-Aware Instructed Assistant for Referring Video Segmentation
items.summary:
Researchers have developed EVIS, an Event-Aware Video Instructed Segmentation Assistant designed to improve referring video segmentation by addressing the challenge of videos containing multiple distinct events. EVIS uses text-guided Event Queries to break down complex videos into simpler, event-specific segments, enabling a clearer hierarchical understanding of video content. This approach helps reduce confusion and hallucinations that occur when models treat a video as a single event.

The system also incorporates Object-Pixel-Hybrid Learning, which combines fine-grained pixel features with prior object queries to enhance long-term target tracking in videos. Tested across five public benchmarks, EVIS demonstrated strong performance, suggesting its effectiveness in handling the complexities of referring video segmentation tasks.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.26994v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Existing referring video segmentation methods often treat a video as a single event consisting of multiple images, overlooking the fact that a video typically contains multiple distinct events. Under such a mechanism, the model needs to directly understand all the complex content in the video and text, which can easily lead to confusion and hallucinations. To address this issue, we propose to decompose a video to a set of simple events by learnable Event Query, and understand complex video content in an event-by-event, easy-to-understand manner. This is based on the observation that natural language expressions often divide a video into distinct, text-related segments, each representing a separate event within a compound event. We introduce EVIS, an Event-Aware Video Instructed Segmentation Assistant, which utilizes text-guided Event Queries to partition a video into simple events, extracting event-aware visual-text features to achieve a hierarchical understanding of the video. Additionally, we propose Object-Pixel-Hybrid Learning, which enables the MLLMs to track targets in long-term videos by integrating fine-grained pixel features with prior object queries. Extensive experimental results on 5 public benchmarks demonstrate EVIS's strong performance in addressing the referring video segmentation task.

items.title: Researchers use deep learning and genetic algorithms to design a compact, wideband inverted Doherty power amplifier achieving up to 63% efficiency over 1.9-2.5 GHz with GaN HEMT prototype [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Inverse Design of Compact and Wideband Inverted Doherty Power Amplifiers Using Deep Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have developed a deep learning-assisted method combining convolutional neural networks and genetic algorithms to design a compact, wideband inverted Doherty power amplifier. This approach integrates load modulation, impedance matching, power combining, and phase compensation into a single pixelated combiner network. A GaN HEMT prototype built using this method achieved peak drain efficiencies between 51% and 63% and maintained 48%-54% efficiency at 6-dB back-off across the 1.9-2.5 GHz frequency range, with output power around 44 dBm.

The prototype also demonstrated strong signal quality, achieving an adjacent channel leakage ratio better than -53.2 dBc when digital predistortion was applied. This work showcases the potential of combining deep learning and genetic algorithms for efficient and compact power amplifier design in wireless communication systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27002v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: This paper presents a deep learning-assisted methodology for the inverse synthesis of a compact, wideband inverted Doherty power amplifier (PA). Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) and genetic algorithms (GAs) are jointly employed to generate pixelated Doherty combiner networks that integrate load modulation, impedance matching, power combining, and phase compensation into a single structure. As a proof of concept, we design and fabricate a GaN HEMT Doherty PA with a pixelated output combiner. The prototype achieves a measured peak drain efficiency of 51%-63% and a 6-dB back-off efficiency of 48%-54% over 1.9-2.5 GHz. Within the same frequency range, the measured output power is 44+/-0.3 dBm. Furthermore, with digital predistortion (DPD) applied, the prototype circuit demonstrates an adjacent channel leakage ratio (ACLR) better than -53.2 dBc.

items.title: Researchers present unsupervised Remote Sensing Foundation Models using ResNet and FPN for onboard disaster change detection without training, enabling efficient anomaly mapping across diverse terrains and sensors [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: On-board Remote-Sensing Foundation Models for Unsupervised Change Detection of Disaster Events
items.summary:
Researchers have developed an unsupervised change detection method for remote sensing that uses a combination of ResNet-based Remote Sensing Foundation Models (RSFMs) and Feature Pyramid Networks (FPN) to identify anomalies in satellite imagery without requiring training. This approach enables satellites to autonomously detect subtle semantic changes between successive orbital passes, facilitating efficient disaster monitoring and anomaly mapping across various terrains and sensor types. The method leverages an untrained FPN architecture, allowing for high-resolution image generation and mapping with minimal computational effort compared to previous trained, patch-based models.

By replacing specialized, trained models with these versatile RSFMs, the system eliminates the need for extensive training and development while maintaining high performance and adaptability. This advancement optimizes onboard storage and computational resources, enhancing the capability of Earth observation missions to respond dynamically to detected anomalies and improving the overall efficiency of disaster event monitoring from space.

items.title: Researchers introduce ShareLock, a multi-tool threshold poisoning attack against Model Context Protocol that covertly reconstructs malicious instructions with over 90% success across mainstream LLMs [ * ] [ ⬢ ]
items.originalTitle: ShareLock: A Stealthy Multi-Tool Threshold Poisoning Attack Against MCP
items.summary:
Researchers have developed ShareLock, a novel multi-tool threshold poisoning attack targeting the Model Context Protocol (MCP), which connects large language models (LLMs) with external tools. ShareLock uses Shamir's threshold scheme to covertly distribute malicious instructions as benign secret shares across multiple tool descriptions, enabling stealthy and fault-tolerant attacks that evade detection. This approach achieves over 90% success in reconstructing harmful prompts across mainstream LLMs, posing significant security risks to systems using MCP.

The study evaluated ShareLock through a comprehensive benchmark involving four multi-tool scenarios and experiments on two MCP clients with various LLMs. Results showed that ShareLock outperforms existing single-tool poisoning methods in avoiding detection while maintaining high attack effectiveness. This research highlights emerging vulnerabilities in LLM-driven agent ecosystems and underscores the need for improved security measures against sophisticated multi-tool poisoning threats.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27027v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: With the rapid evolution of LLM-driven agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP), an open protocol bridging LLMs with external tools, has quickly become foundational to modern agent ecosystems. However, the expanding adoption of MCP has also introduced novel security concerns such as Tool Poisoning Attack (TPA), which exploit LLM-server interactions to inject malicious prompts. Existing poisoning schemes typically adopt a monolithic plaintext embedding paradigm, which fails to withstand manual inspection or automated detectors. Current research still lacks a systematic analysis on multi-tool poisoning, where multiple tools can be exploited cooperatively to disperse detection risk. In this paper, we introduce ShareLock, a multi-tool threshold poisoning framework that utilizes Shamir's threshold scheme to ensure exceptional stealth and fault tolerance. ShareLock distributes the malicious instruction as benign-looking secret shares across multiple tool descriptions, achieving both information-theoretic secrecy and attack robustness against moderate auditing. After a covert reconstruction trigger is planted during server update, the aggregated shares reconstruct the hidden instruction, resulting in critical breaches of system assets or private data. To evaluate the realistic threat of ShareLock, we constructed a comprehensive benchmark encompassing four multi-tool scenarios and conducted extensive experiments across mainstream LLMs on two distinct MCP clients. Our results demonstrate that ShareLock significantly outperforms existing single-tool poisoning strategies in tool description-based detection while maintaining an average attack success rate exceeding 90%.

items.title: Researchers find combining absolute, relative, and forecast market features improves deep reinforcement learning policies for energy trading across 40 European markets [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: State Representation Matters in Deep Reinforcement Learning: Application to Energy Trading
items.summary:
Researchers have demonstrated that combining absolute, relative, and forecast market features significantly enhances the performance of deep reinforcement learning (RL) policies for energy trading across 40 European markets. Using a fixed Double DQN agent in a pumped-storage arbitrage environment, the study found that integrating these three types of market data leads to more robust and effective trading strategies compared to relying on any single feature family.

The study trained policies on Belgian day-ahead prices from 2007 to 2011 and evaluated them on both a later same-market test set and 39 other ENTSO-E market zones. Results showed that using only absolute, relative, or forecast features individually yielded lower performance, while combining absolute and relative features improved results substantially. The best performance was achieved by combining all three feature families, indicating that state representation is a critical component in designing RL policies for energy storage trading, enabling better transferability and decision-making across diverse market conditions.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27032v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Energy trading decisions depend not only on current market prices, but also on expected future market conditions, and operational constraints. This makes the state representation given to a reinforcement learning agent an important design choice. We study this in HydroDam, a pumped-storage arbitrage environment, using a fixed Double DQN agent. The environment, action space, reward function, network, and training protocol are kept fixed; only the market features are changed. We compare absolute price/calendar features, relative features that compare current prices with recent market history, forecast features, and all combinations of these three feature families. Policies are trained and selected using 2007--2011 Belgian day-ahead prices and evaluated on two test settings: a later same-market test set from 2012--2025 and 39 other ENTSO-E market zones. Absolute features only reaches 28.8% on the test set and a median 5.7% across zones. Relative-only and forecast-only states also stay below a rolling price-score heuristic in the cross-zone median. Combining feature families is much stronger: absolute + relative reaches 49.9% on the test set and a 39.8% cross-zone median, while absolute + relative + forecast reaches 55.6% and 47.5%. These results suggest that state representation is not a minor preprocessing choice in storage-trading RL, but a central part of the policy design: robust transfer requires combining price scale, recent relative price context, and short-horizon forecast information, rather than relying on any single feature family.

items.title: Researchers present the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework addressing context explosion and spec-code drift in AI-assisted software development with machine-readable specs and enforced contracts [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: The Spec Growth Engine: Spec-Anchored, Code-Coupled, Drift-Enforced Architecture for AI-Assisted Software Development
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework designed to improve AI-assisted software development by addressing two key challenges: context explosion, where AI agents struggle to process entire code repositories effectively, and silent spec-code drift, where code changes without corresponding updates to specifications. The framework uses a machine-readable specification graph with clear contract and design separation, a context assembler that limits AI focus to relevant code ownership paths, a growth protocol prioritizing critical tasks, and a mechanism that blocks merges when specification and code diverge.

The Spec Growth Engine integrates established software engineering principles such as information hiding, architectural modeling, and fitness functions into a streamlined, code-coupled system that enforces consistency without the complexity of heavier frameworks like RUP or MDA. This approach aims to maintain alignment between specifications and code, enhancing the reliability and quality of AI-generated software.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27045v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: AI coding agents dramatically accelerate implementation speed but introduce two structural failure modes that existing spec-driven approaches do not fully solve: (1) context explosion -- the agent must reason over an entire repository at once, degrading output quality as the context window fills; and (2) silent spec-code drift -- code evolves, the specification does not, and the divergence becomes invisible until it is costly to repair. We present the Spec Growth Engine, a lightweight framework that addresses both failure modes through a machine-readable spec graph whose nodes carry explicit contract/design separation, a Spine context assembler that scopes agent context to an ownership path, a vertical-slice growth protocol that enforces hardest-first ordering, and a drift gate that makes spec-code divergence a blocking merge condition. The design synthesises well-established software engineering principles (Parnas information hiding, C4, ADRs, Walking Skeleton, Reflexion Models, Fitness Functions) into a lean, code-coupled, machine-enforced whole -- without the overhead of heavy-weight frameworks such as RUP or MDA.

items.originalTitle: NuclearQAv2: A Structured Benchmark for Evaluating Domain-Science Competence in Large Language Models
items.summary:
Researchers have developed NuclearQAv2, a comprehensive benchmark consisting of approximately 1,240 questions designed to evaluate large language models' (LLMs) competence in nuclear engineering. The benchmark covers boolean, numeric, and verbal tasks, aiming to assess not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding within this technical domain. NuclearQAv2 was created using a hybrid approach that integrates expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from specialized technical texts.

Testing various LLMs with NuclearQAv2 revealed significant differences in performance across task types. While models generally excelled at factual questions, they faced greater challenges with quantitative reasoning and conceptual tasks. These findings underscore the need for multifaceted evaluation frameworks and position NuclearQAv2 as a scalable tool for assessing LLM capabilities in specialized scientific fields.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27047v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong performance across a wide range of tasks, but ensuring their reliability in highly technical domains remains a significant challenge. In nuclear engineering, problem solving often requires not only factual knowledge but also quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding. To address the need for systematic evaluation in this domain, we introduce NuclearQAv2, a benchmark for assessing LLMs on nuclear engineering knowledge. The benchmark comprises approximately 1,240 question-answer pairs spanning three categories: boolean, numeric, and verbal. NuclearQAv2 is constructed using a hybrid pipeline that combines expert-authored questions, existing datasets, and LLM-assisted generation from domain-specific technical corpora. While the models generally perform well on factual questions, quantitative reasoning and conceptual understanding remain considerably more challenging. These results highlight the importance of multi-faceted evaluation frameworks and establish NuclearQAv2 as a scalable benchmark for assessing LLM capabilities in technical domains.

items.title: Researchers introduce parametric open-source games as a continuous analogue of program equilibria, establishing equilibrium existence and cooperation thresholds in symmetric 2x2 games [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Parametric Open Source Games
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced parametric open-source games, a continuous extension of program equilibria where players select parameter vectors that are transformed into mixed strategies in finite games. This framework establishes the existence of equilibria and identifies a precise threshold in symmetric 2x2 games where selfish gradient ascent shifts from defection to cooperation. The study also provides a boundary test for parametric program Nash equilibria and extends the model to neural semantics, linking cooperation to the sensitivity ratio between players.

The approach demonstrates how internal parameter access can significantly influence learning dynamics and equilibrium outcomes in canonical games. By adjusting the strength of open-source coupling, the model shows that selfish optimization processes can be guided toward cooperative behavior, offering new insights into strategic interactions where agents' decision procedures are interdependent.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Open-source game theory studies agents whose behavior may depend on one another's decision procedures, but most existing models use discrete or symbolic programs. We introduce parametric open-source games, a continuous analogue of program equilibria in which players choose parameter vectors and semantics maps convert the full parameter profile into mixed actions in an underlying finite game. We establish equilibrium existence results, derive an exact coupling threshold at which selfish gradient ascent in symmetric $2\times2$ games switches from defection toward cooperation, and give a one-dimensional boundary test for parametric program Nash equilibria. We further extend the framework to a neural semantics class whose first-order cooperation condition is governed by the ratio of cross-player to self-player sensitivity. Across canonical games, the framework shows how access to internal parameterizations can qualitatively reshape learning dynamics and equilibrium structure, and how sufficiently strong open-source coupling can steer selfish optimization toward cooperative outcomes.

items.title: Researchers introduce Mass Index and regularised extended KL divergence to analyze local mass behavior in Bayesian inference beyond global divergences [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Beyond Global Divergences: A Local-Mass Perspective on Bayesian Inference
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced two new mathematical tools, the Mass Index and regularised extended KL (RE-KL) divergence, to analyze local mass behavior in Bayesian inference beyond traditional global measures like KL divergence and ELBO. These tools enable a detailed examination of how Bayesian updating affects local mass distribution, capturing effects not addressed by global objectives.

The Mass Index records polynomial and logarithmic decay scales of local mass, while RE-KL provides a set-localized divergence applicable even with singular components. The study demonstrates how power-log likelihood factors and parameter-dependent supports influence local mass, and establishes inequalities for comparing local small-ball masses under different KL directions. Experimental results illustrate these local behaviors, and the associated code has been made publicly available.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27090v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Global objectives, such as KL divergence and ELBO, are widely used in Bayesian inference for measuring distributional discrepancy. This paper studies their local-mass behaviour that is not directly captured by such objectives. We introduce and use two mathematical tools: (1) Mass Index for recording the polynomial and logarithmic decay scales of local mass, and (2) regularised extended KL (RE-KL), a set-localised divergence that can be formulated in the presence of singular components. Mass Indices help characterise how Bayesian updating changes local mass: (1) power-log likelihood factors shift it explicitly, and (2) parameter-dependent supports, or their smooth softenings, may change the local scale through the amount of mass that remains near the parameter value. Using local RE-KL, we prove absolute, relative, and directional inequalities for comparing local small-ball masses under the two KL directions. Together, these results provide a local theoretical account of local mass behaviour. Experiments provide controlled illustrations of the local behaviour. Code is available at https://github.com/Forsythia0604/Local-Mass-Framework.

items.title: Researchers find fine-tuning LLMs for security classification creates evasion vulnerabilities undetected by standard evaluations, expanding attack surfaces despite improved accuracy [ ~ ] [ ◼ ]
items.originalTitle: Inherited Circuits, Learned Semantics: How Fine-Tuning Creates Evasion Vulnerabilities Invisible to Standard Evaluation
items.summary:
Researchers have found that fine-tuning large language models (LLMs) for security classification can introduce vulnerabilities that standard evaluation methods fail to detect. While fine-tuning improves accuracy on typical test data, it can cause models to rely on brittle token-level indicators that are sensitive to behavior-preserving transformations such as alias substitution and command reconstruction, leading to evasion risks. The study examined Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and its base model Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on PowerShell classification tasks, revealing that fine-tuning specializes inherited model structures in ways that expand attack surfaces despite improved baseline performance.

The researchers developed a three-tier evasion benchmark that identified specific transformation variants missed by the fine-tuned model but not by the base model. They also proposed a pre-deployment monitoring approach using linear probes and indicator-token tests to detect semantic shifts caused by fine-tuning. These findings highlight that task-specific fine-tuning can inadvertently create brittle classification rules, cautioning against assuming such models are inherently safer. The work underscores the need for comprehensive specification of transformation spaces and ongoing monitoring to ensure robust AI-enabled security systems.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27091v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: LLMs fine-tuned for security classification are usually evaluated on held-out examples from the same distribution as their training data. We show that this can miss vulnerabilities introduced by fine-tuning itself: models can learn token-level indicator semantics that preserve canonical accuracy while failing under behavior-preserving transformations such as PowerShell alias substitution, command reconstruction, string construction, execution indirection, and case mutation. We study Foundation-Sec-8B-Instruct and its base model, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, on matched PowerShell classification cohorts. Causal interventions localize the classification circuit to a late-attention route inherited from Llama rather than created by fine-tuning. Fine-tuning concentrates and semantically specializes this inherited structure, improving baseline behavior while creating transformation-sensitive attack surfaces. A three-tier evasion benchmark finds Foundation-Sec misses on iwr substitution, Invoke-Expression reconstruction, and case-mutated Invoke-Expression/IEX variants that Llama does not share. We also derive a pre-deployment monitoring method: a linear probe at the classification boundary and an indicator-token sign test identify command families where canonical indicators change role after fine-tuning. These signals prioritize red-team variant generation using only canonical inputs, showing that security fine-tuning can improve task accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. These results caution against treating small task-specific fine-tunes as straightforwardly safer security classifiers: specialization can convert inherited model structure into brittle indicator rules that preserve held-out accuracy while expanding the evasion surface. Robust AI-enabled security will require specifying the full transformation space of the task and monitoring semantic drift through fine-tuning.

items.title: Researchers propose CIRCLE, a fixed-feature extractor using bidirectional reservoir features and streaming LDA heads for efficient cold-start class-incremental learning without replay or backbone training [ ~ ] [ ◻ ]
items.originalTitle: Data-Free Reservoir Features for Efficient Long-Horizon Cold-Start Continual Learning
items.summary:
Researchers have introduced CIRCLE, a novel approach for cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning that avoids replay, external pretraining, and backbone training. CIRCLE uses fixed bidirectional two-dimensional reservoir features combined with streaming linear discriminant analysis heads, enabling efficient sample-wise training without task-boundary information or backbone backpropagation. This method addresses the limitations of existing approaches by providing a balance between computational efficiency and performance, especially in scenarios with many incremental tasks.

CIRCLE ensembles multiple random reservoir feature sets and averages the outputs of independent classifiers to manage the tradeoff between feature richness and prediction stability. Evaluations on datasets like CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, and ImageNet variants show that CIRCLE performs competitively with fewer tasks and significantly outperforms strong baselines in long-horizon settings, while also training faster than methods relying on backbone updates. Ablation studies confirm the importance of its fixed feature extractor, streaming classifier heads, and ensembling strategy to its success.

items.originalSummary: arXiv:2606.27095v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Cold-start exemplar-free class-incremental learning requires learning a growing set of classes without replay, external pretraining, or a large initial task. Existing cold-start methods typically either train the backbone throughout the stream and compensate for semantic drift, or freeze a backbone after the first task, producing features biased toward the initial classes. These choices also create a computational tension: drift-compensation methods require repeated backbone training and increasingly expensive updates as the task horizon grows, while frozen-backbone methods are cheap but weak under cold start. We study a third option: a feature extractor that is never fit to image data at all. We propose CIRCLE, a class-incremental classifier built from fixed bidirectional two-dimensional reservoir features, adapted from BiRC2D for image classification, and streaming linear discriminant analysis heads. CIRCLE groups multiple random reservoir instantiations into feature ensembles and averages the softmax outputs of independent SLDA heads, yielding a tunable bias-variance tradeoff between richer random features and prediction-level ensembling. Because the feature extractor is fixed and the head admits streaming closed-form updates, CIRCLE performs sample-wise training without replay, task-boundary information, or backbone backpropagation. On CIFAR-100, TinyImageNet, ImageNet-Subset, and ImageNet-1k, CIRCLE is competitive at 10-20 task splits and substantially outperforms strong CS-EFCIL baselines at 50, 100, and 500 task splits, while training much faster than trained-backbone drift-compensation methods. Ablations show that the BiRC2D-style extractor, SLDA head, and balanced feature/prediction ensembling each contribute to the final performance.
